item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d86TKbcaJEI

值得閱讀的理由

  • 系統性掌握喜馬拉雅資本創辦人李錄歸納的價值投資六大核心原則，深入理解「財富本質是全球購買力份額」的真諦。
  • 看清金融市場中投資者、套利者、投機者與做市商的角色本質，明白股市「教堂附設賭場」的運作邏輯與個人定位。
  • 透視生成式AI從工具邁向自主代理（Agent）的演進軌跡，客觀評估AI在知識整合與實體經濟結構（能源、製造）中的能力邊界。

摘要

價值投資的基石：傳承與創新的六大原則

作者講述了喜馬拉雅資本創辦人李錄在哥倫比亞商學院的精彩分享，將價值投資拆解為六大根本原則。其中前三項承襲自班傑明·葛拉漢：第一，股票代表企業的所有權份額而非單純交易代號；第二，市場是用來服務你而非指導你，報價僅是提供選擇的機會；第三，由於未來不可預測，必須堅持安全邊際以控管風險並提升報酬潛力。

隨後的原則融合了兩位投資宗師與李錄的實務洞察。巴菲特提出了能力圈，其關鍵在於清楚認清自身認知的邊界；蒙格則強調在魚多的地方釣魚，尋求競爭者少且回報更佳的領域。李錄自身增補的第六原則指出，財富本質上是全球購買力的份額，金錢價值會受通膨侵蝕，真正的投資是以合理價格持有具備高能動性的優秀企業，並透過時間複利享受價值創造的成果。

市場生態的劃分與資本市場的核心使命

面對學生對AI時代股票研究員前景的提問，作者轉述李錄對市場參與者的剖析：長期伴隨企業成長的投資者、利用定價偏差獲利的套利者、猜測他人行為的投機者，以及提供流動性的經紀商與做市商。投機屬於總和為零的博弈，其存在源自人性。巴菲特常將市場比喻為附帶賭場的教堂，教堂負責配置資本創造價值，而賭場則伴隨動物本能而生。李錄呼籲投資人應自覺選擇參與價值創造，而非沉溺於零和博弈。

生成式AI的演進浪潮與人類社會的邊界

針對AI的發展，作者指出此波生成式AI正從單純的生產力工具滑向類似獨立物種的光譜。AI在通過圖靈測試後，接連展現出推理、程式編寫能力，並進化為能自主執行的AI代理（Agent）與多代理協同系統。矽谷敘事甚至預言其將透過遞歸自我改進邁向通用人工智慧（AGI）與超級人工智慧（ASI）。然而，李錄認為人類社會絕不會接受由未受控的「人造神」所統治，科技的狂奔終將在社會共識下受到制衡或自我修正。

AI的本質定義與實體經濟的客觀局限

最後，作者分享了對AI技術本質的冷靜審視：AI是依託龐大算力與演算法，在海量人類數據中建立關聯性的鏡像系統。從經濟結構來看，AI高度擅長整合通訊與知識服務層的專業技能，但無法改變能源、交通等底層基礎，亦無法替代由分子與原子重新排列組合的製造業本質。此外，生物界每個細胞所蘊含的資訊複雜度遠超當前數據規模，意味著AI雖是強大的輔助工具，但在實體與生命維度上仍存在著根本的界線。

================================================

Hello everyone, this is Best Partner, I'm Da Fei. Recently, Li Lu, founder and chairman of Himalaya Capital, attended the 36th Graham&Dodd Annual Breakfast at Columbia Business School for an in-depth conversation with Professor Tano Santos, exploring how one should invest. In the dialogue, the first thing he did was break down value investing into six fundamental principles. Among them, three come from Benjamin Graham, who taught at Columbia nearly 90 years ago, one from Buffett, one from Munger, and the final one he added himself. Interestingly, this last. one is the exact opposite of how most people understand wealth. Today, we’d like to share the content of this conversation with you. Li Lu started by noting that value investing originated at Columbia. Graham first taught his course here nearly 90 years ago, though its practice had already existed for a century prior. It has been evolving, but certain core elements remain unchanged. Graham provided three points : first, a stock is part ownership of a business, not just a piece of paper to trade; buying stock is buying a company . Second, the market is there to serve you, not to instruct you; the prices it quotes daily are there to provide you. with opportunities, not to issue you orders. Third, investing is essentially predicting the future, but the future is unpredictable, so you must always demand a margin of safety, which protects against downside and improves upside returns. Buffett’s contribution is the "circle of competence"; we are naturally more interested in certain things, which eventually form expertise, deepened through learning. The most crucial part of the circle of competence is knowing where its boundaries lie. Most people think they know more than they actually do, so recognizing the boundaries is just as important as knowing what is inside the circle. Munger’s principle. is to "fish where the fish are." However, some industries, markets, and companies are crowded with people watching them; when fishermen are crowded together, returns are easily pulled back to average levels, whereas other places receive little attention, have far fewer fishermen, and yield much better results. The sixth principle is the one Li Lu added himself. Over the past 30 years, they have applied value investing globally, and global commerce is also forming a unified market. From this, he reached a realization: wealth, in the end, is simply your share of global purchasing power. It cannot be measured simply by the gold, diamonds, or currency you hold, because inflation causes the purchasing power represented by these. things to erode over time. What truly matters is what you can buy with it. Practically speaking, it means buying excellent, high-energy companies at reasonable prices, giving them enough time to create value, and then sharing in the growth based on your stake. A student asked a very practical question : "Is there still a future for stock research analysts in the AI era?" Li Lu answered in two parts: first, by explaining what investors do, and then by addressing AI separately. He believes market participants generally fall into four categories: one is investors, who accompany companies long-term as they create value; another is arbitrageurs, who profit from. opportunities created by market pricing inaccuracies. In Graham's words, it's buying from pessimists and selling to optimists. A third category is speculators, who mostly guess what others will buy or sell next. They care neither about pricing and value nor about value creation. The remaining category consists of the brokers and market makers who provide trading convenience to the others. Most people don't belong purely to one category but have a bit of each; investment funds simply reflect this average state. Value investors focus on finding a reasonable price and then waiting for a period of time for value to be created. Li Lu notes that Graham leaned more toward the arbitrageur side, whereas Buffett might use arbitrage-style price opportunities, but his primary goal is to participate in value creation. Speculators don't hold long enough to participate in value changes and creation; their aggregate returns are roughly zero, with gains and losses effectively canceling each other out. For society, this is the cost of keeping the market running, as is the case for brokers and market makers. The primary purpose of a market is to channel surplus savings into productive uses, allocating them to worthy companies to create a modern economy capable of compound growth. This is the.

original reason for the stock market's existence. So, why does speculation still exist? Because it is a part of human nature. Buffett often compares the stock market to a church with an attached casino. The church is where value is created, while the casino is practically a required part of obtaining the building permit. When the market was established 400 years ago, it relied on this method to stimulate animal spirits, and 400 years later, it still performs that role. Li Lu told the students, "You need to make a choice: do you want to participate in zero-sum games, or do you want to participate in value creation?" This is a personal choice and a societal one; we must not let the casino expand to. the point of overshadowing the primary purpose for which the market exists. Then there is A, who says this issue is even more complex. He first asks, what exactly is this wave of generative AI? It is clearly a massive wave of technology. Over the past few centuries , we have been dealing with wave after wave of technological change, and the disruption and creation that follow; we have even grasped some of the patterns. But where is the difference this time? On the surface, the speed of change, the scale involved, and the concentrated financial impact at the top are all unprecedented. Going one layer deeper, the momentum this time is different. Previous technologies were basically tools to increase human. productivity, but this round has an extra variable. We are now facing a spectrum from tool to species, and we have begun to move along it. Nearly four years ago, when generative AI was introduced, a moment similar to passing the Turing test occurred. Based on language alone, we can no longer tell whether the one on the other side is a machine or a human. After that, it began to exhibit reasoning capabilities ; reasoning led to programming ability, and with programming ability, it became an agent capable of executing tasks autonomously. Beyond that is the collaboration of multiple agents to complete complex, long-term tasks, just like human society; agents can organize , set priorities, execute tasks in. increasingly complex ways, and even have their own language and communication tools. If you look at the narrative in Silicon Valley, generative AI will next enter the stage of recursive self-improvement (RSI), and it has already partially entered it. The concept is that eventually, all improvements will be completed by the system itself, without the need for human participation, moving from recursive self-improvement to Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), and then to Artificial Super Intelligence (ASI)—its intelligence level will not only exceed any individual but will also exceed the sum of all humanity combined. Pushing further, this is creating some kind of demigod, or an existence similar to a god, except it is man-made. It is so. powerful and all-encompassing that, by this definition, it will inevitably have a huge economic impact, which justifies all kinds of investment costs . When a trillion-dollar initial public offering appears, it is as if everyone is being invited to participate in the IPO of a god. But A, stepping back, asks: If things are really like this, what will happen to humanity? We will live in a society ruled by a man-made god, where only a very small number of people can access it, no one can truly understand it, and it cannot even be said that anyone can control it. Would anyone be willing to live in such a society? His answer is clear: No. In. his view, there are only two outcomes: either this technology doesn't actually move in that direction, or it truly does. Then, at some point, we will all unite to prevent it from becoming such an existence. In either case, we will not allow an uncontrolled artificial god to rule over human society. Setting that aside, is AI a useful technology? Bill's answer is quite straightforward; he provides a definition: it is a machine that, through immense computing power and refined algorithms, builds systemic, mirror-based correlations among near-infinite variables using all. human-generated and derivative data, thus forming an ability that covers a significant portion of human reasoning and intelligence. We know how it works and how to make it better, but we don't yet fully understand why it is able to function this way. Looking at the present through this definition, it is narrowing the capability gap at certain levels. Bill layered the economic structure: the bottom level is energy and transportation, followed by manufacturing, then communications and digital media, and above that, a vast array of knowledge-based and technical services. He claims AI is very adept at integrating knowledge and expertise at.

this level, making these capabilities accessible to more people, but it cannot change fundamental areas like energy and transport, nor does it change the nature of manufacturing. Manufacturing is essentially the recombination of different molecules and atoms, so AI's room for growth lies in the communications and digital layer , but it has not surpassed humans; we remain within the scope of human-generated data. To enter that level in a biological sense, one needs to bridge a completely different order of magnitude. Bill gave an example. Every one of our cells contains what could be called 50 gigabytes of data; to reach our biological level, that. would have to be multiplied by trillions. However, the capabilities AI has already formed have indeed begun to shift the balance between tools and species. In theory, either of the two aforementioned scenarios is enough to make one believe that recursive self-improvement without human participation and oversight is dangerous; it will form its own goals and sub-goals for its own purposes, further drifting from human control. He emphasizes that in "recursive self-improvement," who exactly defines the improvement and who controls the meaning and direction of progress— human or machine—is the most critical red line at present. Just as the technology is useful and transformative , it is also dangerous, and as a. society, we must collectively establish a red line. Whether through autonomous learning or using tools, it cannot be separated from human participation and supervision; it must be kept on the side of being a tool. It will bring massive shocks, ranging from employment and emotional dependency to various risks in cyber, biological, and nuclear fields. Lee also specifically pointed out that this technology always generates incremental costs. Previous technologies allowed for one-time investment with long-term amortization, but this technology does not. Each additional unit of usage comes with new costs; thus, costs, revenue, and profit are critical. Capital requirements and financial discipline will always play a. role, and when considering the pace of progress, one must account for four or five different levels of factors simultaneously, including development speed and societal capacity for adaptation. Human society has never adapted to change by planning in advance; we will experience tremendous booms and busts, and perhaps even more. Guest added an observation: since this technology is extraordinary and dangerous, and we do not fully understand why it generates certain answers, human participation in verification is mandatory. Ultimately, what determines the flow of economic rent is the scarcity of this skill, and how rare the talent capable of supervising AI output truly is. If you. are smart enough and can effectively communicate with AI in a specific field , you yourself will become a scarce resource, and economic rent will likely flow toward you. Lee’s response is that there might be nuanced differences at various levels, but we shall wait and see. He then shifted the topic to the market itself. He showed students a chart: the market capitalization of the largest company divided by GDP. This ratio was historically between 2%and 4% , but now, with Nvidia, it has reached about 15%. He asked, as the market becomes increasingly dependent on a few companies, how should one build a portfolio to protect oneself from the shocks of this technology? Lee’s. answer was quite simple. He said, "The market will always do strange things, and you don't have to be dictated by the market's behavior at any given moment." This is one of Benjamin Graham's most important insights. He then talked about a prospectus he recently read: a company claiming to be a research lab that has already burned through tens of billions of dollars and promises to burn through hundreds of billions more. It promises to provide a transformative technology while admitting there is a 10%chance it could lead to human extinction, and then invites people to invest at least $ 100 billion at a $ 2 trillion valuation. Lee said the contradictions here are too obvious; both claims cannot be true. simultaneously, yet that is the reality . Some things are fundamentally irrational and unsustainable, and they will not go on forever. Looking at centuries of market history, this has always been the pattern. He cited the S &P index as an example, noting that over the 16 years since 2010, the average annualized return was 14%to 15% , while the 10 years prior, from 2000 to 2010, saw an average return of exactly zero, or in fact, slightly negative. When you combine the past 26 years, the average return sits in the high single digits. In the long run, this figure is generally reasonable, assuming real GDP growth of about 2%.

plus 2%to 3%inflation, totaling 4%to 5% growth; listed companies perform slightly better, especially the 500 firms that remain after continuous screening. For instance, this should serve as a basic pillar: investors will eventually receive returns commensurate with their investments, and the market will return to rationality over time, though this process is interrupted by periods of extremism. So, what does this divergence mean? At any given moment, the market cannot create massive amounts of new capital out of thin air; if capital flows overwhelmingly to the very top, it means many inherently excellent companies are trading at very low. prices. This is true in the US, China, and elsewhere; China may be more extreme, but over time, the market’s weighing machine will determine long-term investor returns. For example , this divergence actually leaves better opportunities for rational people, provided you can remain rational, which is very difficult. It is easy to get caught up, especially in a massive technological wave where your imagination is stretched, speculation becomes more active, and exaggeration turns more extreme; but for rational people, these situations create even better long-term investment opportunities. The host then asked about China, noting the fluctuations of. the past few years and the problems in real estate and banking that recall situations elsewhere, so how should one view the Chinese market now? First, let's discuss the background: the Chinese stock market has remained largely stagnant over the past decade. Ten years ago, China reached a middle-income level; the question is how to break through. Many countries stall at this level, to the point where a term was coined to describe it: the " middle-income trap," with dozens of countries failing to advance after 40 or 50 years. As a large economy, it is natural to ask what exactly keeps a middle-income country stuck under the ceiling and unable to move up. So, China began consciously shifting its. economy from low-to-mid-end manufacturing toward mid-to-high-end manufacturing, introducing not a five-year plan, but a ten-year plan called "Made in China 2025," which outlined about ten major goals. A few years into the plan's implementation, the first Trump administration took office and launched a trade war, which further reinforced China's assessment. Not only was the natural path unlikely to break the ceiling, but other countries might also intentionally keep China confined under it. After Trump came Biden, who kept the trade tariffs and added even more restrictions. About halfway through the timeline, around 2021, China further increased investment. Beyond pushing for the. transformation of manufacturing, it added goals for technological self-reliance, especially in fields with real bottlenecks like semiconductors, large aircraft engines, and operating system software code. The list of bottlenecks at that time was very long. What followed was another five years of ramping up and accelerating. In short, when you try to achieve goals that seem impossible and that many other countries haven't reached, you inevitably have to pay a heavy price. This has always been China's way of developing its economy: setting major goals at different stages while bearing the corresponding, massive costs. One of the main costs over the past five years has been the. balance sheets and household wealth of the Chinese middle class, as housing prices peaked in 2021. A typical Chinese middle-class family has about 70%of its net assets tied to housing, and this housing carries about 50% leverage through mortgages. In the five years since then and up to now, national housing prices have fallen by about 40%on average, and the total wealth of these families has dropped by 60%to 70%on average. In such a situation, people do three things: reduce consumption, increase savings, and pay off debt as much as possible. The result is that the growth of consumption and domestic demand has slowed, and today the growth rate is roughly at zero. Savings deposits have. risen to about 120%of GDP, which is approximately 165 trillion yuan. People have also experienced two or three years where prices basically didn't rise or slightly declined, so there are concerns about confidence when looking toward the future. This is one facet of the economy, but on another level, the path is different: China's manufacturing sector finally broke through the low-to-mid end and steadily moved into the mid-to-high end. Every goal of "Made in China 2025" has been basically achieved, and there has been significant progress in resolving bottleneck issues over the past five years. Take semiconductors as an example: the logical assessment is that the U.S.-led technology sanctions actually became a golden opportunity for China's semiconductor industry,.

because it gave the industry one of the most precious things in a market economy: demand. If you ask any entrepreneur what is most important, they will all say it is orders. With demand and revenue, the cycle begins to turn. More revenue brings profit, profit supports R&D, R&D drives improvement, and improvement leads to even more revenue. This cycle continues to advance until, in mature process fields, China has achieved near-complete self-sufficiency in both equipment and chip manufacturing. In more advanced processes, it is also nearing self-sufficiency, with only a few key bottlenecks left to solve. This is only one aspect. A core capability. of generative AI is its ability to produce intelligence at scale, and one of its greatest applications is generating code, which happens to be perfect for solving major bottleneck issues. Primarily, this addresses missing operating system code layers. From PCs to servers, to semiconductors, and NVIDIA's CUDA systems, these segments are now being replaced one by one with AI's help, making it an essential tool for closing capability gaps. Over the past decade, China has taken a dominant position in fields like new energy, electric vehicles, energy storage batteries, and heavy machinery, becoming a global leader and. narrowing the gap in areas where bottlenecks persist. Meanwhile, other industries have paid a very heavy price . Take real estate as an example; measured by annual new home sales, the market has now fallen by roughly 70%. The reduced 10 trillion RMB happens to be equivalent to the amount invested annually in manufacturing upgrades and technological efficiency improvements. This shift in capital flow occurred around 2021. Looking back at China's development over the past 50 years, this has consistently been its development model. The goals of one decade sometimes become the costs of the next. In the early days of industrial takeoff, the environment, air quality, and rivers were the costs. sacrificed. Later, they became the targets for improvement, and polluting enterprises became the side paying the price. During urbanization, real estate developers were a key force in achieving goals. They built today's China and formed the foundation of the middle class's wealth, but in the last five to ten years, they have become the side paying the price. The process involves a lot of pain, but overall, the country has indeed made progress through these stages. This is why a development process spanning hundreds of years could be compressed into 40 years. However, at any point in time, as an investor or entrepreneur, you must always know one thing: are you the. goal to be supported in this stage, or the cost that must be paid to achieve that goal? The overall assessment is that a country with such massive economic and demographic scale has finally embarked on a path of comprehensive modernization; however, due to a dual-layered economic divergence and a general lack of confidence, the financial market has stagnated for a decade, with virtually no progress. At the same time, you can see some excellent companies with extreme global competitiveness trading at very low prices. If you are a rational investor who can see the full picture, you might form a different perspective. In today's market, you are very likely to find better investment opportunities than at other times. The. final major question asked by the host is about the world. He said that when he founded Himalaya Capital in 1997, the world was open and crossed borders, with a generous and open spirit that seems to be missing today; for example, the world has indeed changed over the past 30 years. The time scale for changes in the world order is very long ; the formation and transformation of an order require decades, sometimes even centuries. The current world order was formed after two world wars. Post-war, a U.S.-led order emerged, which became a unified order after the Cold War, and now it is shifting again toward an order that has not yet taken. shape and remains unclear to us. Yet, beneath it lies another order that has been steadily forming over the past few centuries: the economic order, where an increasing number of countries and populations participate in shared trade , forming a common market. About 30 years ago, with the collapse of the Soviet Union and the end of the Cold War, this common market finally formed, and almost all countries and populations joined the same market economic system. This economic system has a characteristic: once a common market is formed, it is difficult for any country to voluntarily withdraw. With the flywheel of efficiency and continuous improvement brought by the market, any country that withdraws for a long time must pay a huge price. Once.

formed, it is difficult to disintegrate , and it will last for a much longer time. For example, in the trade wars and friction of the past 100 years, no matter what barriers are set, people can always find trade routes through third countries and still follow comparative advantages. Taking U.S.- China trade as an example, direct trade has certainly declined, but if you add up U.S. trade with Mexico and ASEAN, the increased portion exactly offsets it. U.S.-China trade is basically still at its original scale; it has simply been rerouted through third countries. At the level of world order, the United States has led the globe for 80 years, bearing most of the costs to ensure that the economic common market operates in the way it deems appropriate. Later, it realized that. the costs and benefits might not be proportional, so it voluntarily withdrew from some responsibilities, but so far it has not been very successful and has left a vacuum. The single biggest change in the world order is the rise of China over the last thirty or forty years. It has become a massive economy with a complete manufacturing system, is achieving technological autonomy, and possesses the world’s largest unified market with open, standardized regulations. Li Lu shared a very interesting observation here: in the field of generative AI, everyone needs semiconductor chips, but where are these chips manufactured? Think about those countries that produce chips; they have one thing in common: all the. countries and people that produce these semiconductor chips use chopsticks. He added, "India doesn't produce semiconductor chips and doesn't use chopsticks," for instance, in the manufacturing phase. Moreover, the people leading semiconductor companies in this country also use chopsticks, from Jensen Huang to Lip-Bu Tan, to Lisa Su, and even to Patrick Gelsinger —it's the same for all of them. He said that our interdependence is very deep. If a country or a company wants to bet on this new technology on a large scale as they are doing now, they must be friendlier to those who use chopsticks. This will not change, because it did not happen by accident. He also mentioned that the U.S. President and the Chinese President met four times in eight months, and one of the most important outcomes of these meetings was often just scheduling the next one. This reflects a kind of strategic stability. At the same time, all parties are competing fiercely, and they all believe that time is on their side. China wants to achieve semiconductor autonomy, the U.S. wants an AI breakthrough, and other countries have their own plans. Peace and stability are crucial for every side, and the largest countries have both the responsibility and the willingness to maintain them. Li Lu also made a distinction between two types of AI paths. In his view, U.S. AI companies focus more on exploring the technological frontier. They ask themselves, "What else can this. technology do?""How far can the boundaries be pushed?""That is why they keep referring to themselves as research laboratories." While Chinese AI companies are equally curious, they tend to ask a different question: "What can this technology do for my customers ?" This includes both individual consumers and corporate clients. Regarding cryptocurrency, Li Lu was more direct. He said he doesn't take it seriously at all and believes it will eventually disappear on its own because it is fundamentally a sham. A currency that can realize its value is guaranteed by the force behind it. Without such a mechanism, you cannot establish a reliable measure for. settlement or a store of wealth. It is easily used for illegal transactions, and he even believes that banning it would make life better for everyone. Of course, some people want to collect it, just as some believe a certain artist's work is worth a certain price; that is a personal preference, but from a societal perspective, he doesn't think it has any value. In the final Q&A session, the host took questions from the floor. Someone asked if value investing principles could apply to growth or high-tech firms, and another asked what the fusion of energy and intellectual capital means for the climate and environment. Someone else asked how to face the professional pressure of underperforming, which is a very real risk in the investment. industry. Another person asked what the most important thing he had learned over the past ten years was. What made him better than he was ten years ago? Also, when evaluating an investment, how do you ensure a sufficient margin of safety and downside protection, and what are the most important structural changes in the US and Chinese capital markets? His response began with a judgment: all intelligent investing is value investing, because you always want to get slightly more than what you pay for. You pay a price and receive value, regardless of where that value manifests—whether it is in a stagnant or even declining business that returns large amounts of cash to you, or a.

rapidly growing company. Or perhaps it is an investment with a low probability of success and a high probability of failure, which therefore requires specific odds and a return differential . It all comes down to your understanding of where value is created . The fundamental principle is the discounting of future cash flows, provided you can understand those cash flows and make accurate estimates. As for the pressure of underperformance, he said this is indeed a very realistic issue; you subscribe to this philosophy , and naturally, you hope the market will cooperate with you. This is human nature; everyone wants the best of both worlds, wanting to participate in the long term while hoping to report beautiful performance results every. single year. But as soon as you think this way, it won't be long before you turn into a speculator. You cannot have it both ways; you either believe the market is there to instruct you, or you believe the market is there to serve you. Anyone who wants to mix these two up is better off doing index investing, because an index is exactly the average result of all market participants. To truly build a career, you must find people who share your philosophy and are willing to support you consistently . The difficulty of this industry lies in the fact that you must, to a significant extent, act against human nature. The reason you believe you are right is that logic and facts support you, not because others agree or disagree with you. Some people are. suited for this; if you determine that you are not, then do not force it. You can't just say, "I want to have the biggest fund and reach a certain scale. " That’s not how things work; ultimately, you will get results that are commensurate with everything you have done. As for the margin of safety and downside protection, a key difference between value investors and most others is the extreme emphasis placed on protecting the downside. Investing is about predicting the future, but the future is unpredictable . All you can do is invest in what you truly understand, and what you know is often very limited. He starts with things he knows for certain and can verify, like balance sheets—much like. the Graham approach—and moves from the simple to the more complex. This is how a circle of competence naturally develops: you must understand its boundaries while consciously expanding it over time. If your knowledge can achieve consistent compound growth, then eventually your capital will, too. Every decade, he finds that he has learned so much. By doing the right things in the right way and truly achieving compound growth, the results are astounding. The problem with zero-sum games is that what you learn today might be useless tomorrow. You can't accumulate knowledge, so you become increasingly dependent on. non-human means. At some point, you will be replaced—so as a human, where does your value lie? For example, his mentor, partner, and teacher Munger always advocated for one thing: the highest form of human relationship is a seamless web of trust formed by people who are reliable to one another. He suggests that everyone starting their career should move toward this way of life. He acknowledges that some may have better luck, but as long as you choose the right partners and things worth doing, the effects of compounding are incredible. It may take many years, but by moving forward slowly and steadily, you will eventually reach a. position that corresponds to your efforts. The basic philosophy of compounding is not to lose what you already have. So, don't lose your knowledge, don't lose the relationships built on trust, don't lose your wisdom, and don't even lose your health. Looking at the conversation as a whole, I feel the logic consistently stands on the same principle: start from the value you truly understand, protect the downside, and let knowledge and trust accumulate together. So, in this market where a tiny number of companies drive the technological frontier and values are severely distorted, are you willing. to participate in a zero-sum game, or are you willing to engage in value creation? This question may have no standard answer, but it will determine your...

李录在哥伦比亚商学院第36届格雷厄姆与多德年度午餐会上的完整访谈。他把价值投资归结为六条原则，从格雷厄姆的三条基础理念，到巴菲特的能力圈、芒格的"到有鱼的地方钓鱼"，再到他自己补充的"财富是全球购买力的份额"。他正面回应AI时代：技术非常有用，但技术前景不能替代投资回报的计算；他明确反对脱离人类监督的递归自我改进，认为必须用一条红线把AI限定在"工具"这一侧。谈到市场，他用一份"半神IPO"式招股书说明非理性，用标普26年数据说明长期回报终将回归企业盈利。对中国，他用"目标与代价"解释产业升级与居民信心之间的分化，以及股市为何可能成为下一个财富载体。他也对全球化、共同市场、筷子观察与加密货币给出了自己的判断。

item.description:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d86TKbcaJEI

值得閱讀的理由

  • 系統性掌握喜馬拉雅資本創辦人李錄歸納的價值投資六大核心原則，深入理解「財富本質是全球購買力份額」的真諦。
  • 看清金融市場中投資者、套利者、投機者與做市商的角色本質，明白股市「教堂附設賭場」的運作邏輯與個人定位。
  • 透視生成式AI從工具邁向自主代理（Agent）的演進軌跡，客觀評估AI在知識整合與實體經濟結構（能源、製造）中的能力邊界。

摘要

價值投資的基石：傳承與創新的六大原則

作者講述了喜馬拉雅資本創辦人李錄在哥倫比亞商學院的精彩分享，將價值投資拆解為六大根本原則。其中前三項承襲自班傑明·葛拉漢：第一，股票代表企業的所有權份額而非單純交易代號；第二，市場是用來服務你而非指導你，報價僅是提供選擇的機會；第三，由於未來不可預測，必須堅持安全邊際以控管風險並提升報酬潛力。

隨後的原則融合了兩位投資宗師與李錄的實務洞察。巴菲特提出了能力圈，其關鍵在於清楚認清自身認知的邊界；蒙格則強調在魚多的地方釣魚，尋求競爭者少且回報更佳的領域。李錄自身增補的第六原則指出，財富本質上是全球購買力的份額，金錢價值會受通膨侵蝕，真正的投資是以合理價格持有具備高能動性的優秀企業，並透過時間複利享受價值創造的成果。

市場生態的劃分與資本市場的核心使命

面對學生對AI時代股票研究員前景的提問，作者轉述李錄對市場參與者的剖析：長期伴隨企業成長的投資者、利用定價偏差獲利的套利者、猜測他人行為的投機者，以及提供流動性的經紀商與做市商。投機屬於總和為零的博弈，其存在源自人性。巴菲特常將市場比喻為附帶賭場的教堂，教堂負責配置資本創造價值，而賭場則伴隨動物本能而生。李錄呼籲投資人應自覺選擇參與價值創造，而非沉溺於零和博弈。

生成式AI的演進浪潮與人類社會的邊界

針對AI的發展，作者指出此波生成式AI正從單純的生產力工具滑向類似獨立物種的光譜。AI在通過圖靈測試後，接連展現出推理、程式編寫能力，並進化為能自主執行的AI代理（Agent）與多代理協同系統。矽谷敘事甚至預言其將透過遞歸自我改進邁向通用人工智慧（AGI）與超級人工智慧（ASI）。然而，李錄認為人類社會絕不會接受由未受控的「人造神」所統治，科技的狂奔終將在社會共識下受到制衡或自我修正。

AI的本質定義與實體經濟的客觀局限

最後，作者分享了對AI技術本質的冷靜審視：AI是依託龐大算力與演算法，在海量人類數據中建立關聯性的鏡像系統。從經濟結構來看，AI高度擅長整合通訊與知識服務層的專業技能，但無法改變能源、交通等底層基礎，亦無法替代由分子與原子重新排列組合的製造業本質。此外，生物界每個細胞所蘊含的資訊複雜度遠超當前數據規模，意味著AI雖是強大的輔助工具，但在實體與生命維度上仍存在著根本的界線。

================================================

Hello everyone, this is Best Partner, I'm Da Fei. Recently, Li Lu, founder and chairman of Himalaya Capital, attended the 36th Graham&Dodd Annual Breakfast at Columbia Business School for an in-depth conversation with Professor Tano Santos, exploring how one should invest. In the dialogue, the first thing he did was break down value investing into six fundamental principles. Among them, three come from Benjamin Graham, who taught at Columbia nearly 90 years ago, one from Buffett, one from Munger, and the final one he added himself. Interestingly, this last. one is the exact opposite of how most people understand wealth. Today, we’d like to share the content of this conversation with you. Li Lu started by noting that value investing originated at Columbia. Graham first taught his course here nearly 90 years ago, though its practice had already existed for a century prior. It has been evolving, but certain core elements remain unchanged. Graham provided three points : first, a stock is part ownership of a business, not just a piece of paper to trade; buying stock is buying a company . Second, the market is there to serve you, not to instruct you; the prices it quotes daily are there to provide you. with opportunities, not to issue you orders. Third, investing is essentially predicting the future, but the future is unpredictable, so you must always demand a margin of safety, which protects against downside and improves upside returns. Buffett’s contribution is the "circle of competence"; we are naturally more interested in certain things, which eventually form expertise, deepened through learning. The most crucial part of the circle of competence is knowing where its boundaries lie. Most people think they know more than they actually do, so recognizing the boundaries is just as important as knowing what is inside the circle. Munger’s principle. is to "fish where the fish are." However, some industries, markets, and companies are crowded with people watching them; when fishermen are crowded together, returns are easily pulled back to average levels, whereas other places receive little attention, have far fewer fishermen, and yield much better results. The sixth principle is the one Li Lu added himself. Over the past 30 years, they have applied value investing globally, and global commerce is also forming a unified market. From this, he reached a realization: wealth, in the end, is simply your share of global purchasing power. It cannot be measured simply by the gold, diamonds, or currency you hold, because inflation causes the purchasing power represented by these. things to erode over time. What truly matters is what you can buy with it. Practically speaking, it means buying excellent, high-energy companies at reasonable prices, giving them enough time to create value, and then sharing in the growth based on your stake. A student asked a very practical question : "Is there still a future for stock research analysts in the AI era?" Li Lu answered in two parts: first, by explaining what investors do, and then by addressing AI separately. He believes market participants generally fall into four categories: one is investors, who accompany companies long-term as they create value; another is arbitrageurs, who profit from. opportunities created by market pricing inaccuracies. In Graham's words, it's buying from pessimists and selling to optimists. A third category is speculators, who mostly guess what others will buy or sell next. They care neither about pricing and value nor about value creation. The remaining category consists of the brokers and market makers who provide trading convenience to the others. Most people don't belong purely to one category but have a bit of each; investment funds simply reflect this average state. Value investors focus on finding a reasonable price and then waiting for a period of time for value to be created. Li Lu notes that Graham leaned more toward the arbitrageur side, whereas Buffett might use arbitrage-style price opportunities, but his primary goal is to participate in value creation. Speculators don't hold long enough to participate in value changes and creation; their aggregate returns are roughly zero, with gains and losses effectively canceling each other out. For society, this is the cost of keeping the market running, as is the case for brokers and market makers. The primary purpose of a market is to channel surplus savings into productive uses, allocating them to worthy companies to create a modern economy capable of compound growth. This is the.

original reason for the stock market's existence. So, why does speculation still exist? Because it is a part of human nature. Buffett often compares the stock market to a church with an attached casino. The church is where value is created, while the casino is practically a required part of obtaining the building permit. When the market was established 400 years ago, it relied on this method to stimulate animal spirits, and 400 years later, it still performs that role. Li Lu told the students, "You need to make a choice: do you want to participate in zero-sum games, or do you want to participate in value creation?" This is a personal choice and a societal one; we must not let the casino expand to. the point of overshadowing the primary purpose for which the market exists. Then there is A, who says this issue is even more complex. He first asks, what exactly is this wave of generative AI? It is clearly a massive wave of technology. Over the past few centuries , we have been dealing with wave after wave of technological change, and the disruption and creation that follow; we have even grasped some of the patterns. But where is the difference this time? On the surface, the speed of change, the scale involved, and the concentrated financial impact at the top are all unprecedented. Going one layer deeper, the momentum this time is different. Previous technologies were basically tools to increase human. productivity, but this round has an extra variable. We are now facing a spectrum from tool to species, and we have begun to move along it. Nearly four years ago, when generative AI was introduced, a moment similar to passing the Turing test occurred. Based on language alone, we can no longer tell whether the one on the other side is a machine or a human. After that, it began to exhibit reasoning capabilities ; reasoning led to programming ability, and with programming ability, it became an agent capable of executing tasks autonomously. Beyond that is the collaboration of multiple agents to complete complex, long-term tasks, just like human society; agents can organize , set priorities, execute tasks in. increasingly complex ways, and even have their own language and communication tools. If you look at the narrative in Silicon Valley, generative AI will next enter the stage of recursive self-improvement (RSI), and it has already partially entered it. The concept is that eventually, all improvements will be completed by the system itself, without the need for human participation, moving from recursive self-improvement to Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), and then to Artificial Super Intelligence (ASI)—its intelligence level will not only exceed any individual but will also exceed the sum of all humanity combined. Pushing further, this is creating some kind of demigod, or an existence similar to a god, except it is man-made. It is so. powerful and all-encompassing that, by this definition, it will inevitably have a huge economic impact, which justifies all kinds of investment costs . When a trillion-dollar initial public offering appears, it is as if everyone is being invited to participate in the IPO of a god. But A, stepping back, asks: If things are really like this, what will happen to humanity? We will live in a society ruled by a man-made god, where only a very small number of people can access it, no one can truly understand it, and it cannot even be said that anyone can control it. Would anyone be willing to live in such a society? His answer is clear: No. In. his view, there are only two outcomes: either this technology doesn't actually move in that direction, or it truly does. Then, at some point, we will all unite to prevent it from becoming such an existence. In either case, we will not allow an uncontrolled artificial god to rule over human society. Setting that aside, is AI a useful technology? Bill's answer is quite straightforward; he provides a definition: it is a machine that, through immense computing power and refined algorithms, builds systemic, mirror-based correlations among near-infinite variables using all. human-generated and derivative data, thus forming an ability that covers a significant portion of human reasoning and intelligence. We know how it works and how to make it better, but we don't yet fully understand why it is able to function this way. Looking at the present through this definition, it is narrowing the capability gap at certain levels. Bill layered the economic structure: the bottom level is energy and transportation, followed by manufacturing, then communications and digital media, and above that, a vast array of knowledge-based and technical services. He claims AI is very adept at integrating knowledge and expertise at.

this level, making these capabilities accessible to more people, but it cannot change fundamental areas like energy and transport, nor does it change the nature of manufacturing. Manufacturing is essentially the recombination of different molecules and atoms, so AI's room for growth lies in the communications and digital layer , but it has not surpassed humans; we remain within the scope of human-generated data. To enter that level in a biological sense, one needs to bridge a completely different order of magnitude. Bill gave an example. Every one of our cells contains what could be called 50 gigabytes of data; to reach our biological level, that. would have to be multiplied by trillions. However, the capabilities AI has already formed have indeed begun to shift the balance between tools and species. In theory, either of the two aforementioned scenarios is enough to make one believe that recursive self-improvement without human participation and oversight is dangerous; it will form its own goals and sub-goals for its own purposes, further drifting from human control. He emphasizes that in "recursive self-improvement," who exactly defines the improvement and who controls the meaning and direction of progress— human or machine—is the most critical red line at present. Just as the technology is useful and transformative , it is also dangerous, and as a. society, we must collectively establish a red line. Whether through autonomous learning or using tools, it cannot be separated from human participation and supervision; it must be kept on the side of being a tool. It will bring massive shocks, ranging from employment and emotional dependency to various risks in cyber, biological, and nuclear fields. Lee also specifically pointed out that this technology always generates incremental costs. Previous technologies allowed for one-time investment with long-term amortization, but this technology does not. Each additional unit of usage comes with new costs; thus, costs, revenue, and profit are critical. Capital requirements and financial discipline will always play a. role, and when considering the pace of progress, one must account for four or five different levels of factors simultaneously, including development speed and societal capacity for adaptation. Human society has never adapted to change by planning in advance; we will experience tremendous booms and busts, and perhaps even more. Guest added an observation: since this technology is extraordinary and dangerous, and we do not fully understand why it generates certain answers, human participation in verification is mandatory. Ultimately, what determines the flow of economic rent is the scarcity of this skill, and how rare the talent capable of supervising AI output truly is. If you. are smart enough and can effectively communicate with AI in a specific field , you yourself will become a scarce resource, and economic rent will likely flow toward you. Lee’s response is that there might be nuanced differences at various levels, but we shall wait and see. He then shifted the topic to the market itself. He showed students a chart: the market capitalization of the largest company divided by GDP. This ratio was historically between 2%and 4% , but now, with Nvidia, it has reached about 15%. He asked, as the market becomes increasingly dependent on a few companies, how should one build a portfolio to protect oneself from the shocks of this technology? Lee’s. answer was quite simple. He said, "The market will always do strange things, and you don't have to be dictated by the market's behavior at any given moment." This is one of Benjamin Graham's most important insights. He then talked about a prospectus he recently read: a company claiming to be a research lab that has already burned through tens of billions of dollars and promises to burn through hundreds of billions more. It promises to provide a transformative technology while admitting there is a 10%chance it could lead to human extinction, and then invites people to invest at least $ 100 billion at a $ 2 trillion valuation. Lee said the contradictions here are too obvious; both claims cannot be true. simultaneously, yet that is the reality . Some things are fundamentally irrational and unsustainable, and they will not go on forever. Looking at centuries of market history, this has always been the pattern. He cited the S &P index as an example, noting that over the 16 years since 2010, the average annualized return was 14%to 15% , while the 10 years prior, from 2000 to 2010, saw an average return of exactly zero, or in fact, slightly negative. When you combine the past 26 years, the average return sits in the high single digits. In the long run, this figure is generally reasonable, assuming real GDP growth of about 2%.

plus 2%to 3%inflation, totaling 4%to 5% growth; listed companies perform slightly better, especially the 500 firms that remain after continuous screening. For instance, this should serve as a basic pillar: investors will eventually receive returns commensurate with their investments, and the market will return to rationality over time, though this process is interrupted by periods of extremism. So, what does this divergence mean? At any given moment, the market cannot create massive amounts of new capital out of thin air; if capital flows overwhelmingly to the very top, it means many inherently excellent companies are trading at very low. prices. This is true in the US, China, and elsewhere; China may be more extreme, but over time, the market’s weighing machine will determine long-term investor returns. For example , this divergence actually leaves better opportunities for rational people, provided you can remain rational, which is very difficult. It is easy to get caught up, especially in a massive technological wave where your imagination is stretched, speculation becomes more active, and exaggeration turns more extreme; but for rational people, these situations create even better long-term investment opportunities. The host then asked about China, noting the fluctuations of. the past few years and the problems in real estate and banking that recall situations elsewhere, so how should one view the Chinese market now? First, let's discuss the background: the Chinese stock market has remained largely stagnant over the past decade. Ten years ago, China reached a middle-income level; the question is how to break through. Many countries stall at this level, to the point where a term was coined to describe it: the " middle-income trap," with dozens of countries failing to advance after 40 or 50 years. As a large economy, it is natural to ask what exactly keeps a middle-income country stuck under the ceiling and unable to move up. So, China began consciously shifting its. economy from low-to-mid-end manufacturing toward mid-to-high-end manufacturing, introducing not a five-year plan, but a ten-year plan called "Made in China 2025," which outlined about ten major goals. A few years into the plan's implementation, the first Trump administration took office and launched a trade war, which further reinforced China's assessment. Not only was the natural path unlikely to break the ceiling, but other countries might also intentionally keep China confined under it. After Trump came Biden, who kept the trade tariffs and added even more restrictions. About halfway through the timeline, around 2021, China further increased investment. Beyond pushing for the. transformation of manufacturing, it added goals for technological self-reliance, especially in fields with real bottlenecks like semiconductors, large aircraft engines, and operating system software code. The list of bottlenecks at that time was very long. What followed was another five years of ramping up and accelerating. In short, when you try to achieve goals that seem impossible and that many other countries haven't reached, you inevitably have to pay a heavy price. This has always been China's way of developing its economy: setting major goals at different stages while bearing the corresponding, massive costs. One of the main costs over the past five years has been the. balance sheets and household wealth of the Chinese middle class, as housing prices peaked in 2021. A typical Chinese middle-class family has about 70%of its net assets tied to housing, and this housing carries about 50% leverage through mortgages. In the five years since then and up to now, national housing prices have fallen by about 40%on average, and the total wealth of these families has dropped by 60%to 70%on average. In such a situation, people do three things: reduce consumption, increase savings, and pay off debt as much as possible. The result is that the growth of consumption and domestic demand has slowed, and today the growth rate is roughly at zero. Savings deposits have. risen to about 120%of GDP, which is approximately 165 trillion yuan. People have also experienced two or three years where prices basically didn't rise or slightly declined, so there are concerns about confidence when looking toward the future. This is one facet of the economy, but on another level, the path is different: China's manufacturing sector finally broke through the low-to-mid end and steadily moved into the mid-to-high end. Every goal of "Made in China 2025" has been basically achieved, and there has been significant progress in resolving bottleneck issues over the past five years. Take semiconductors as an example: the logical assessment is that the U.S.-led technology sanctions actually became a golden opportunity for China's semiconductor industry,.

because it gave the industry one of the most precious things in a market economy: demand. If you ask any entrepreneur what is most important, they will all say it is orders. With demand and revenue, the cycle begins to turn. More revenue brings profit, profit supports R&D, R&D drives improvement, and improvement leads to even more revenue. This cycle continues to advance until, in mature process fields, China has achieved near-complete self-sufficiency in both equipment and chip manufacturing. In more advanced processes, it is also nearing self-sufficiency, with only a few key bottlenecks left to solve. This is only one aspect. A core capability. of generative AI is its ability to produce intelligence at scale, and one of its greatest applications is generating code, which happens to be perfect for solving major bottleneck issues. Primarily, this addresses missing operating system code layers. From PCs to servers, to semiconductors, and NVIDIA's CUDA systems, these segments are now being replaced one by one with AI's help, making it an essential tool for closing capability gaps. Over the past decade, China has taken a dominant position in fields like new energy, electric vehicles, energy storage batteries, and heavy machinery, becoming a global leader and. narrowing the gap in areas where bottlenecks persist. Meanwhile, other industries have paid a very heavy price . Take real estate as an example; measured by annual new home sales, the market has now fallen by roughly 70%. The reduced 10 trillion RMB happens to be equivalent to the amount invested annually in manufacturing upgrades and technological efficiency improvements. This shift in capital flow occurred around 2021. Looking back at China's development over the past 50 years, this has consistently been its development model. The goals of one decade sometimes become the costs of the next. In the early days of industrial takeoff, the environment, air quality, and rivers were the costs. sacrificed. Later, they became the targets for improvement, and polluting enterprises became the side paying the price. During urbanization, real estate developers were a key force in achieving goals. They built today's China and formed the foundation of the middle class's wealth, but in the last five to ten years, they have become the side paying the price. The process involves a lot of pain, but overall, the country has indeed made progress through these stages. This is why a development process spanning hundreds of years could be compressed into 40 years. However, at any point in time, as an investor or entrepreneur, you must always know one thing: are you the. goal to be supported in this stage, or the cost that must be paid to achieve that goal? The overall assessment is that a country with such massive economic and demographic scale has finally embarked on a path of comprehensive modernization; however, due to a dual-layered economic divergence and a general lack of confidence, the financial market has stagnated for a decade, with virtually no progress. At the same time, you can see some excellent companies with extreme global competitiveness trading at very low prices. If you are a rational investor who can see the full picture, you might form a different perspective. In today's market, you are very likely to find better investment opportunities than at other times. The. final major question asked by the host is about the world. He said that when he founded Himalaya Capital in 1997, the world was open and crossed borders, with a generous and open spirit that seems to be missing today; for example, the world has indeed changed over the past 30 years. The time scale for changes in the world order is very long ; the formation and transformation of an order require decades, sometimes even centuries. The current world order was formed after two world wars. Post-war, a U.S.-led order emerged, which became a unified order after the Cold War, and now it is shifting again toward an order that has not yet taken. shape and remains unclear to us. Yet, beneath it lies another order that has been steadily forming over the past few centuries: the economic order, where an increasing number of countries and populations participate in shared trade , forming a common market. About 30 years ago, with the collapse of the Soviet Union and the end of the Cold War, this common market finally formed, and almost all countries and populations joined the same market economic system. This economic system has a characteristic: once a common market is formed, it is difficult for any country to voluntarily withdraw. With the flywheel of efficiency and continuous improvement brought by the market, any country that withdraws for a long time must pay a huge price. Once.

formed, it is difficult to disintegrate , and it will last for a much longer time. For example, in the trade wars and friction of the past 100 years, no matter what barriers are set, people can always find trade routes through third countries and still follow comparative advantages. Taking U.S.- China trade as an example, direct trade has certainly declined, but if you add up U.S. trade with Mexico and ASEAN, the increased portion exactly offsets it. U.S.-China trade is basically still at its original scale; it has simply been rerouted through third countries. At the level of world order, the United States has led the globe for 80 years, bearing most of the costs to ensure that the economic common market operates in the way it deems appropriate. Later, it realized that. the costs and benefits might not be proportional, so it voluntarily withdrew from some responsibilities, but so far it has not been very successful and has left a vacuum. The single biggest change in the world order is the rise of China over the last thirty or forty years. It has become a massive economy with a complete manufacturing system, is achieving technological autonomy, and possesses the world’s largest unified market with open, standardized regulations. Li Lu shared a very interesting observation here: in the field of generative AI, everyone needs semiconductor chips, but where are these chips manufactured? Think about those countries that produce chips; they have one thing in common: all the. countries and people that produce these semiconductor chips use chopsticks. He added, "India doesn't produce semiconductor chips and doesn't use chopsticks," for instance, in the manufacturing phase. Moreover, the people leading semiconductor companies in this country also use chopsticks, from Jensen Huang to Lip-Bu Tan, to Lisa Su, and even to Patrick Gelsinger —it's the same for all of them. He said that our interdependence is very deep. If a country or a company wants to bet on this new technology on a large scale as they are doing now, they must be friendlier to those who use chopsticks. This will not change, because it did not happen by accident. He also mentioned that the U.S. President and the Chinese President met four times in eight months, and one of the most important outcomes of these meetings was often just scheduling the next one. This reflects a kind of strategic stability. At the same time, all parties are competing fiercely, and they all believe that time is on their side. China wants to achieve semiconductor autonomy, the U.S. wants an AI breakthrough, and other countries have their own plans. Peace and stability are crucial for every side, and the largest countries have both the responsibility and the willingness to maintain them. Li Lu also made a distinction between two types of AI paths. In his view, U.S. AI companies focus more on exploring the technological frontier. They ask themselves, "What else can this. technology do?""How far can the boundaries be pushed?""That is why they keep referring to themselves as research laboratories." While Chinese AI companies are equally curious, they tend to ask a different question: "What can this technology do for my customers ?" This includes both individual consumers and corporate clients. Regarding cryptocurrency, Li Lu was more direct. He said he doesn't take it seriously at all and believes it will eventually disappear on its own because it is fundamentally a sham. A currency that can realize its value is guaranteed by the force behind it. Without such a mechanism, you cannot establish a reliable measure for. settlement or a store of wealth. It is easily used for illegal transactions, and he even believes that banning it would make life better for everyone. Of course, some people want to collect it, just as some believe a certain artist's work is worth a certain price; that is a personal preference, but from a societal perspective, he doesn't think it has any value. In the final Q&A session, the host took questions from the floor. Someone asked if value investing principles could apply to growth or high-tech firms, and another asked what the fusion of energy and intellectual capital means for the climate and environment. Someone else asked how to face the professional pressure of underperforming, which is a very real risk in the investment. industry. Another person asked what the most important thing he had learned over the past ten years was. What made him better than he was ten years ago? Also, when evaluating an investment, how do you ensure a sufficient margin of safety and downside protection, and what are the most important structural changes in the US and Chinese capital markets? His response began with a judgment: all intelligent investing is value investing, because you always want to get slightly more than what you pay for. You pay a price and receive value, regardless of where that value manifests—whether it is in a stagnant or even declining business that returns large amounts of cash to you, or a.

rapidly growing company. Or perhaps it is an investment with a low probability of success and a high probability of failure, which therefore requires specific odds and a return differential . It all comes down to your understanding of where value is created . The fundamental principle is the discounting of future cash flows, provided you can understand those cash flows and make accurate estimates. As for the pressure of underperformance, he said this is indeed a very realistic issue; you subscribe to this philosophy , and naturally, you hope the market will cooperate with you. This is human nature; everyone wants the best of both worlds, wanting to participate in the long term while hoping to report beautiful performance results every. single year. But as soon as you think this way, it won't be long before you turn into a speculator. You cannot have it both ways; you either believe the market is there to instruct you, or you believe the market is there to serve you. Anyone who wants to mix these two up is better off doing index investing, because an index is exactly the average result of all market participants. To truly build a career, you must find people who share your philosophy and are willing to support you consistently . The difficulty of this industry lies in the fact that you must, to a significant extent, act against human nature. The reason you believe you are right is that logic and facts support you, not because others agree or disagree with you. Some people are. suited for this; if you determine that you are not, then do not force it. You can't just say, "I want to have the biggest fund and reach a certain scale. " That’s not how things work; ultimately, you will get results that are commensurate with everything you have done. As for the margin of safety and downside protection, a key difference between value investors and most others is the extreme emphasis placed on protecting the downside. Investing is about predicting the future, but the future is unpredictable . All you can do is invest in what you truly understand, and what you know is often very limited. He starts with things he knows for certain and can verify, like balance sheets—much like. the Graham approach—and moves from the simple to the more complex. This is how a circle of competence naturally develops: you must understand its boundaries while consciously expanding it over time. If your knowledge can achieve consistent compound growth, then eventually your capital will, too. Every decade, he finds that he has learned so much. By doing the right things in the right way and truly achieving compound growth, the results are astounding. The problem with zero-sum games is that what you learn today might be useless tomorrow. You can't accumulate knowledge, so you become increasingly dependent on. non-human means. At some point, you will be replaced—so as a human, where does your value lie? For example, his mentor, partner, and teacher Munger always advocated for one thing: the highest form of human relationship is a seamless web of trust formed by people who are reliable to one another. He suggests that everyone starting their career should move toward this way of life. He acknowledges that some may have better luck, but as long as you choose the right partners and things worth doing, the effects of compounding are incredible. It may take many years, but by moving forward slowly and steadily, you will eventually reach a. position that corresponds to your efforts. The basic philosophy of compounding is not to lose what you already have. So, don't lose your knowledge, don't lose the relationships built on trust, don't lose your wisdom, and don't even lose your health. Looking at the conversation as a whole, I feel the logic consistently stands on the same principle: start from the value you truly understand, protect the downside, and let knowledge and trust accumulate together. So, in this market where a tiny number of companies drive the technological frontier and values are severely distorted, are you willing. to participate in a zero-sum game, or are you willing to engage in value creation? This question may have no standard answer, but it will determine your...

李录在哥伦比亚商学院第36届格雷厄姆与多德年度午餐会上的完整访谈。他把价值投资归结为六条原则，从格雷厄姆的三条基础理念，到巴菲特的能力圈、芒格的"到有鱼的地方钓鱼"，再到他自己补充的"财富是全球购买力的份额"。他正面回应AI时代：技术非常有用，但技术前景不能替代投资回报的计算；他明确反对脱离人类监督的递归自我改进，认为必须用一条红线把AI限定在"工具"这一侧。谈到市场，他用一份"半神IPO"式招股书说明非理性，用标普26年数据说明长期回报终将回归企业盈利。对中国，他用"目标与代价"解释产业升级与居民信心之间的分化，以及股市为何可能成为下一个财富载体。他也对全球化、共同市场、筷子观察与加密货币给出了自己的判断。
