值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入解析黃仁勳於柏林 GTC 大會揭示的「AI 是製造業」核心戰略與全球產業五層架構。
  • 全面剖析 NVIDIA 突破摩爾定律極限、十年實現效能百萬倍激增的「極致協同設計」與次世代全液冷 Rubin 架構。
  • 掌握 AI Agent 生產力爆發下的安全挑戰，以及 NVIDIA 提出的作業系統級開源安全解決方案 OpenSecure。

摘要

算力十年百萬倍躍進與 NVIDIA 歐洲戰略

作者大飛回顧十年前黃仁勳親自將重達需兩人抬上樓的 DGX-1 超級電腦交付給 OpenAI，如今僅需單手就能舉起具備相同規格的筆記型電腦。十年間 AI 運算效能實現了驚人的百萬倍增長，遠超摩爾定律預期的百倍上限。本次 GTC 大會首度移師德國柏林，展現 NVIDIA 深耕歐洲 33 年的底蘊；在過去一年中，NVIDIA 不僅向歐洲注資近百億美元，更攜手施耐德電機、西門子能源及多家歐洲新創，全面推動歐洲產業邁入 AI 時代。

AI 的製造業本質與分散式工廠布局

黃仁勳在演講中指出當前 AI 發展的核心觀點：「AI 不是軟體，而是製造業」。他勾勒出 AI 產業的五層蛋糕模型：由底層的能源與高效能運算、第二層的 AI 工廠、第三層產出 Token（智慧）的模型，到最上層將智慧嵌入各產業硬體與服務。此外，他預測未來的電信基地台與資料中心將整合為超過十萬個節點、總計 100GW 的分散式 AI 網路，打破算力高度集中於少數超大規模資料中心的現狀。

全棧極致協同設計與 Rubin 革命性硬體

NVIDIA 將自身重新定義為「加速演算法的演算法公司」，依靠晶片、系統結構與軟體算法同步重構的極致協同設計，持續推動效能滾雪球式躍升。最新發表的 Rubin 架構相較前代實現巨大突破，不僅達到百分之百全液冷且內部無任何裸露線纜，節點組裝時間更從兩小時驟降至五分鐘以內。搭配與台積電合作的光學共封裝交換機 Spectrum-X 與原廠預製整合的 DGX SuperPOD，能將 AI 工廠的部署週期縮短數月，並顯著降低三成的能耗與大量冷卻水消耗。

Agent 生產力崛起與作業系統級 OpenSecure 防護

隨著具備推理與工具調用能力的智慧體（Agent）全面爆發，黃仁勳解析了構成 Agent 的五大支柱：模型大腦、外骨骼治理架構、安全沙箱、知識庫以及執行工具。為了解決提示詞層面防護權限濫用的不足，NVIDIA 推出開源的 OpenSecure 執行環境，透過作業系統層級的策略管理、外部獨立進程注入憑證與沙箱隔離機制，從根本杜絕金鑰外洩與越權行為，為未來的企業級 Agent 生態提供堅實防禦。

================================================

Hello everyone, this is Best Partner, I am Da Fei. Ten years ago, Jensen Huang personally delivered a machine so heavy it took two people to carry upstairs to OpenAI's office. This machine was the DGX-1, NVIDIA's first-ever AI supercomputer, featuring 128GB of memory and one petaflop of computing power. Yet on the GTC stage in Berlin last week, he held up a laptop with that same 128GB of memory and the same one petaflop of performance with just one hand. AI performance has surged a million-fold in ten years. Under Moore's Law, it would have increased. 100-fold at most; that extra 10,000- fold difference is what we’re discussing today. This Berlin GTC marks the first time NVIDIA has moved its main stage to Europe. You might not know that NVIDIA has been deeply rooted in Europe for 33 years. The RIVA 128 chip, which almost bankrupted the company in its early days, was actually made in France. Back then, Silicon Graphics was their largest workstation client, which helped NVIDIA break into the graphics workstation market. Audi was also the very first automaker to adopt NVIDIA’s in-vehicle computing systems. In the past year, they have poured nearly $ 10 billion into Europe,. announcing investments in 14 European startups just the week before the speech. Schneider Electric and Siemens Energy are both collaborating with NVIDIA. SAP, Revolut, Spotify, Porsche, and more—a whole string of European giants are leaning into the AI economy. The conference opened, as always, with Jensen Huang’s keynote address. The core takeaway from this speech can be summarized in one sentence: AI is not software; it is manufacturing. He sketched out a simple five-layer cake for the AI industry: the bottom layer is energy-powered high-performance computers; the next layer up is the AI factory where these computers cluster; above that, the factories run models to continuously output tokens, or intelligence. Finally, these tokens are embedded into the hardware and services of every industry. Each of these five layers is driving job creation and economic growth. Schneider and Siemens Energy lead globally in the energy layer, Mistral and other European firms have a foothold in models, and startups like Nebius are rising fast in the AI factory layer. Huang also made a prediction: in the future, every global telecom company will have over 100,000 sites, totaling about 100 gigawatts of distributed telecom base stations and data centers, evolving into a. decentralized AI network. This means AI infrastructure will no longer be concentrated solely in a few hyperscale data centers. So, where does NVIDIA fit into this five-layer cake? Most people think of GPUs first, but today NVIDIA is more than just a GPU company; from GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage, and switch chips to system software, CUDA libraries, models, and tools, they have products at almost every level. Jensen Huang defined the company this way: We are an algorithm company that develops chips to accelerate those algorithms.

He mentioned extreme co-design, which translated means every architectural upgrade isn't just swapping in a faster chip, but redesigning the chip, architecture, system form factor, and system software algorithms all at once. New algorithms force them to change the architecture, and the new architecture pushes the algorithms further, creating a snowball effect. This is why Moore's Law could only achieve a 100-fold increase, while NVIDIA has achieved a million-fold increase. Across six generations of architecture, from Pascal in 2016 to the current Rubin, every generation has pushed boundaries. Blackwell is about 30 times faster than Hopper, and two years later, Rubin will. be another 30 times faster than Blackwell. The Rubin computer looks completely different from previous products; it has no cables, no wires, and is 100%liquid-cooled. It used to take two hours to assemble a DGX Blackwell node, with wires everywhere, but now assembling a Rubin node takes less than 5 minutes. Each GPU has 20 petaflops of compute power, using NVLink switches to connect 72 GPUs into one massive computer. He pulled this thing out directly during the live stream to show the audience, saying, " Now you know this isn't a special effect." The supporting networking equipment also received a revolutionary. upgrade; Spectrum-X is the world's first co-packaged optics Ethernet switch. Traditional solutions use printed circuit boards to transmit data , where bandwidth and signal quality are significantly compromised. So, NVIDIA and TSMC co-developed a process to package optics directly onto the chip, allowing data to move from the laser into the transceiver and then straight to the chip, bypassing the bottleneck of circuit boards. Currently , the mass-produced specification is 512 ports, each at 200 Gbps. The scale of an AI factory is massive, with a 1- gigawatt facility costing about $ 50 billion. It usually takes months from. construction to operation, but Jensen Huang announced DGX SuperPOD, where the entire AI facility is pre-fabricated in the factory. It contains seven liquid-cooled computer racks, using 17 kilometers of Spectrum-X cabling to interconnect into a Rubin NVL72 compute unit. All of this is completely wired and tested in the factory, then packed into containers and shipped to the site , where it can be started simply by connecting local power. Let’s do the math: for an AI factory with an expected annual revenue of $ 40 billion , a three-month delay in production means a $ 10 billion loss. DXP can compress the time from delivery to. token output from four or five months down to about one month. Electricity and water are saved too; the accompanying DXS Maxlps is a dynamic control loop that can adjust power supply in real-time based on the workload. While maintaining the same performance, it saves 30%in power. Regarding the cooling system, NVIDIA supports a closed-loop liquid cooling system with a maximum temperature of 45 degrees Celsius, and in suitable climates, it can even use outdoor dry coolers to dissipate heat, eliminating water evaporation entirely. If calculated at a gigawatt scale, it could save 54 million liters of water per day, equivalent to the daily water consumption of 180,000 households. Of.

course, hardware alone is not enough; you also need software to get the factory up and running. Jensen said that an AI factory itself is a miracle, and to light it up, power it on, and start producing tokens requires an incredibly massive software ecosystem. Because it provides a complete full-stack software suite, from underlying system software to top-level CX, he then turned the topic to agents. Over the past year, AI has undergone a real transformation: agents have begun to possess productivity. At the beginning of the year, OpenCloud introduced the concept of open-source agents, kicking off a global wave of agent scaling. Agents began to think,. reason, iterate, and use tools; consumption skyrocketed, and the demand for GPUs truly exploded. Then, he provided a structural definition: agents are composed of five elements. One is the model; the model is responsible for perception. Reasoning, planning, and acting—this is the agent's brain. The second is the agent's harness, which he directly calls the agent's exoskeleton. The model is the brain, and the harness is the rest of the body; it is used to coordinate workflows, manage active, working, and long-term memory, and activate tools. Because the open-source NICE it provides supports OC and HMERS,. the third element is the sandbox, which is the secure, isolated environment for the harness to run in. The fourth element is knowledge, provided by the Agent Knowledge Foundation, allowing agents to read and understand an enterprise's structured and unstructured data. The fifth element is tools, carried by the C library's X library, enabling agents to execute specific computational tasks. His judgment is that in the future, there won't be just one model running all tasks; every company will use a mix of closed models, open-source models, and custom-trained models, choosing the most suitable one based on the type of task. And then, we reach a very important announcement from this speech. : OpenShare. Wang Xun stated that the current way of preventing agents from abusing permissions is essentially just adding a line in the prompt: "Please do not delete anything." He played a self-deprecating video on stage that started with this scene, then concluded : that is not security. OpenSecure is an open-source secure runtime environment released by NVIDIA in late September, based on the Apache 2.0 license. Its core design philosophy is to place secure execution outside of the agent itself. Policies are enforced at the operating system level, because security barriers inside large language models are unreliable. The specific mechanism of OpenSecure is divided into. three layers; the first is the policy layer. You can use YAML to define which files each agent can access and which network endpoints it can connect to, with OpenSecure enforcing these policies at the system call level. Next is credentials; the agent itself does not hold any secret keys. We run an independent process, the Supervisor, outside the sandbox to keep all credentials secure. Only when a request is approved by the policy does the Supervisor inject the credentials into that request. A compromised agent cannot leak secret keys because it never possessed them in the first place . The third is the isolation layer; each agent runs in an independent.

sandbox with no direct network access, and all outbound requests must be checked by the Supervisor. Compare OpenSecure to the browser sandbox of the early internet. SQL-Agent then performs predictive analysis on structured databases. The system can predict which orders will be affected and by how long, and then use vector database search to find technical documents for replacement parts. CUDA-X is the result of over 20 years of accumulated accelerated computing libraries, covering more than 350 fields such as fluid dynamics, particle physics, quantum chemistry, image processing, data processing, and ray. tracing. He compared CUDA to the SQL of the AI industry, believing that for the AI industry, CUDA holds the same significance as SQL does for the global database industry, just as OpenGL and DirectX did for the real-time computer graphics industry; CUDA birthed the AI computing industry. Two agents from DST and Volkswagen collaborated to convert a Golf car door to an automated mechanism ; NVIDIA analyzed the requirements, a simulator ran the simulations, and after discovering vibration issues, the design was automatically corrected. He believes the exact opposite: after the arrival of AI. , there will be more users of these tools than ever before. Every tool company will become an AI company, providing not just software, but also specially optimized agents that are extremely proficient at using their tools. He first talked about telecommunications networks, which is one of the best examples of physical AI. Cell towers can use radio waves to perceive the world, perform reasoning, and use. beamforming to interact with it, which is structurally identical to what robots do with cameras and actuators. Huang applied AI technology used in ray tracing to wireless communications, enabling a million-to-one level improvement in spectral efficiency. In terms of infrastructure, approximately 100,000 telecom sites worldwide and 100 gigawatts of distributed data centers will evolve into a decentralized AI network in the future. a patient's tumor changes shape during the process, the robot can perceive the changing bodily environment in real time, precisely segment the tumor boundaries, and dynamically adjust the radiation direction. In the future , platforms like Uber, Bolt, Grab, and Lyft will feature robotaxis, but they won't come from just one brand. Building autonomous driving systems is. extremely expensive, especially the software component, which is why NVIDIA decided to create a standardized architecture. Hyperion's standard configuration includes 14 cameras, nine radars, three lidars, and numerous ultrasonic sensors, all driven by two NVIDIA GPU systems. What NVIDIA aims to do is create a virtual fleet. standard that any brand can join. In this presentation, four new NVIDIA partners and vehicle models chose to join, including Volkswagen, the Volvo fleet, the next-generation Mercedes-Benz, and new models from Jaguar Land Rover. item.itunes:author: 最佳拍档
item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RNdnfCpQTZU

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入剖析 DeepSeek 開源的 DeepInf 推理架構，理解大模型從靜態權重轉化為高併發線上服務的工程內幕。
  • 掌握 PD 分離（Prefill 與 Decoding 分離）設計思維，了解如何依照算力與顯存頻寬需求，異質佈署高效能叢集。
  • 揭示巨幅降低推論成本的核心密碼：透過 KV Cache 前綴匹配與 3FS 分布式儲存，將吞吐效能提升 25 倍並兼顧系統容錯能力。

摘要

開源引擎的戰略轉變與三大組件佈局

作者大飛指出，DeepSeek 正式開源了支撐其線上服務的推論框架 DeepInf 與編碼組件 DeepSeek-Recipe。傳統觀點常認為模型開源僅是釋出權重檔案，但權重就像食譜，若沒有強大的後廚工程團隊（推論引擎）負責排隊與排程調度，便無法即時產出回答。過去 DeepSeek 曾因高度客製化與維護成本考量而不願開放內部引擎，如今不僅推翻前態全面開源，還聯同先前的 Search 與 Fetch 工具構建了完整閉環：由檢索工具抓取乾淨食材、DeepInf 統籌算力烹飪，並由 DeepSeek-Recipe 擔任翻譯多國語言訂單的菜單。

DeepSeek-Recipe 的協議轉換與防禦機制

為解決 OpenAI 與 Anthropic 等主流 API 格式互不相容的問題，以 Rust 打造的 DeepSeek-Recipe 提供了轉譯機制，將外部請求標準化為內部對話格式並編碼為 tokens。該組件內建跨資料區塊解析的狀態機，解決 UTF-8 中文字與工具參數在資料流中被切碎的問題。此外，Recipe 僅在建構 Prompt 時將結構標籤映射為特殊標籤，若使用者手動輸入相同字元則視為普通文字，巧妙修補了假冒系統指令的注入漏洞，同時支援開啟思考模式下最高 131,072 tokens 的深度推理輸出。

PD 分離架構與硬體極致調度

在推論生命週期中，運算被嚴格拆分為 Prefill（預填） 與 Decoding（解碼） 兩大階段。Prefill 需要一次性吸收大量歷史紀錄與系統提示，極度消耗純算力；Decoding 則是逐字生成，效能瓶頸在於自顯存讀取參數與快取的頻寬。DeepSeek 藉此落實了徹底的 PD 分離：Prefill 採用 8 卡伺服器集中攻堅，Decoding 分配給 64 至 128 卡的運算叢集，而視覺編碼器則獨立交由廉價單卡處理。透過針對不同特性的階段配置相應硬體，實現了首字延遲與接續輸出速率的最佳化。

KV Cache 前綴快取與 3FS 分布式儲存架構

在多輪對話與 Agent 工具調用中，重複傳輸的歷史脈絡耗費巨大，DeepSeek 透過 KV Cache 前綴匹配 實現極致省流。命中快取後，單卡 Prefill 吞吐量能從每秒 6 萬 tokens 激增至 150 萬 tokens，成本僅需未命中的五十分之一。這些快取被統一存放在容量達 100PB 的 3FS 分布式儲存系統 中，針對對話流量保留長達七天以捕捉長尾命中率。計算與儲存分離的架構不僅消除了單機故障遺失快取的風險，更結合 GDR 與 RDMA 技術，在運算進行時無縫搬移資料，將推論成本與延遲壓榨至極限。

================================================

Hello everyone, welcome to Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. On October 20th , DeepSeek open-sourced its inference framework, DeepInf, which powers its online services, along with its companion encoding component, DeepSeek-Recipe. This time, DeepSeek didn’t release a new model or climb the leaderboards; instead, they handed over the blueprints for the engine behind the model. Today, let’s talk about this framework. To understand it, we first need to clarify what an inference framework actually is. Many think open-sourcing a model just means downloading the weights, and that's it. But weights are just a pile of numbers; they can't talk or answer questions. In. between lies an entire engineering stack responsible for queuing requests, feeding them into the chips, and retrieving the results. Tech blogger Baoyu once used the analogy of a cookbook and a kitchen staff. If the model file is the recipe, the inference framework is the kitchen staff. Give the same recipe to different kitchen crews, and the number of orders they can handle per hour—and how long customers wait—can vary significantly . That’s why open-sourcing an engine is much rarer than open-sourcing weights. Open weights are now routine, but open-sourcing an engine means showing everyone how you staff your kitchen and how you scale operations. In April 2025, DeepSeek explained why they wouldn’t open their internal engine, essentially saying it was heavily customized for their environment and hard to migrate, and that the team didn't have the resources to maintain a large public project. However, by this October, they overturned that stance. They released more than one repository; besides DeepInf, there’s also DeepSeek-Recipe . Just a few days before that, DeepSeek launched Search and Fetch tools specifically for models. While these three things seem scattered, they are actually connected. Search and Fetch go out to source ingredients, DeepInf is the kitchen crew, and Recipe serves as. a multi-lingual menu, allowing orders in various formats to be translated into a language the kitchen understands . Let’s briefly touch on Search and Fetch, which are backed by a layer people rarely consider. We all know search engines are designed for humans, filled with ads, recommendations, and pop-ups that we can easily ignore. But models can’t; every extra word consumes context, uses tokens, and costs money. These two APIs return raw JSON data. Beyond providing titles, URLs, summaries, full text, and timestamps, they also include relevance. and authority scores. It’s quite simple: you provide a URL, and it returns cleaned-up Markdown data. The two APIs are priced at 5 yuan per 1,000 successful requests, and users can call them using server-side tools in depsharnessCodecodex. There is no charge before November 1, 2026, at 0:00 Beijing Time. It also doesn't require binding a specific model; you only need a Depsik API to call models from other providers. Of course, the real star is deepINF, which adopts the Apache 2.0 license. It supports NVIDIA's SM100 and Huawei's Ascend 950, requiring a Linux. environment with Python 3.12 and GCC 13 or higher. On the NVIDIA side, it requires CUDA 13, and for Ascend, it needs CANN 9.2. Currently, it only supports one model: depsicv 4.1 flash, with the weight code for pulling being depsicv 4.1 flash 1017. We will go into the specific logging details later. Next is deepsicrecipe, which solves format issues. Currently, there are three mainstream APIs: OpenAI chat completions and responses, as well as Anthropic messages. Ultimately, they all ask the model for answers, but the formats differ, so you cannot directly.

port the same conversation. If you want to run deepsake on your own server but write the client based on OpenAI standards, the model won't understand. Therefore, a translator is needed in between. RP handles this translation; its core is written in Rust, with a Python interface provided. It unifies all three types of requests into an internal conversation format, constructs prompts according to the model version, and encodes them into tokens using its built-in tokenizer. After the model outputs, it restores the tokens back into a response following the corresponding protocol and streams it back to the user. It also maintains a cross-data-block parsing state machine. Since a Chinese. character takes three bytes in UTF-8, it could be split across two adjacent blocks, as could tool parameters. Thus, it waits for data before parsing, ensuring the user never sees half a character. It also happens to patch a security vulnerability. Deps models rely on a set of special tokens to mark conversation structures, such as where a user's statement begins or when a tool is called. If someone manually types the exact same user or image tags in their input, they could impersonate the system and issue commands. Recipe's approach is to only map tags explicitly inserted during prompt construction. into special tokens; the same strings typed by a user are treated as ordinary text. Additionally, when thinking mode is disabled, the output limit defaults to 8,192 tokens. With thinking mode enabled, it is 65,536, and if the reasoning intensity is set to maximum, it can reach 131,072. Now, let’s look at an example to see how a request goes through the entire process. First, a request must pass through the tokenizer to become tokens, then it splits into two stages. The first stage is called prefill, where the model reads system prompts, chat history, and document. questions all at once; each token generates a set of intermediate results at every layer, known as the KV cache. The second stage is decoding, where it generates one token at a time; each new token produced requires using all the previous KV caches. These two stages consume completely different resources: prefill processes tens of thousands of tokens at once, demanding pure compute power, while decoding generates one token at a time, spending most of its time reading parameters and cache from VRAM. Therefore, DeepSeek splits them onto different machines, which is the commonly known PD separation. When this system was designed, three goals were set: compatibility with different. vendors 'chips, enabling commodity hardware for prefill and decoding, and keeping the KV cache for at least an hour. In deployment, prefill uses 8-GPU servers, decoding uses 64 to 128-GPU clusters, and the vision encoder is pulled out separately; each of the three stages gets its own resources, optimizing first-token and inter-token latency separately. The official documentation has an interesting note: the vision encoder usually only needs a single card, and they suggest using the cheapest available card. In actual deployment, the ratio of cards for the two stages is close to 1: 1; while a. minimum setup of one prefill unit and one decoding unit can run, efficient performance requires following the official starting scale. Next is the most cost-saving part of the entire system. In agent scenarios, every time a tool is called, the client must resend the complete history—system prompts, tool definitions, and every previous response and tool result—not a single bit can be missed. Yet, the vast majority of these have actually been calculated in the previous turn. DeepSeek’s approach is to cache the computed KV values, so in the next turn , it only calculates the newly added tokens. The requirement is that the prefix must match exactly to hit the.

cache, so it must align from the first token; repeated content starting in the middle cannot be used. How dramatic is the effect of this caching? On the same card, without cache hits, prefill can process 60,000 tokens per second; with cache hits, it’s 1.5 million—a 25- fold difference. The average input per request for Deps online is 77K, with an average time-to-first-token latency of 400ms, and a P99 of 1000ms. The cost of input with a cache hit is only 1/50th of a miss; for every point the hit rate increases, the bill gets thinner. These caches aren't stored in the compute machine's own memory, but in an independent storage cluster using. DeepSeg's previously open-sourced distributed file system, 3FS, with a capacity of about 100PB on SSDs, writing KV caches in blocks of 128 tokens. Cache for ENT traffic is kept for three days, while chat traffic is kept for seven days. Chat traffic is kept longer due to its long-tail hit characteristics, where a small amount of cache is read repeatedly, so losing it has a bigger impact on the overall hit rate. Based on Deck's estimates, if they only kept it for three days, the chat traffic hit rate would drop by 0.5 %to 1%. Looking at the industry, OpenAI and Google only keep caches for about 5 minutes to 24 hours, so three to seven. days is considered quite long. Storing them in an independent cluster has two benefits: any compute machine can read any piece of cache, so users are no longer locked to the previous machine. The failure rate of compute machines is also several orders of magnitude higher than storage, so even if a machine crashes, the cache remains. However, reading the cache shouldn't drag down the time-to-first-token latency, so DPS divides hits into three stages: the first stage, at the ingress service, uses a hash chain to perform prefix matching on the local KV store to get metadata. To hit the length, the second stage must fetch the data before. routing, using an independent process to move the cache from 3FS into host shared memory, while the third stage, the engine layer, moves it from shared memory to VRAM, overlapping layer-by-layer transfer with forward computation. They could have used a large copy engine, but the copy performance for fine-grained blocks wasn't ideal, so DPS switched to GDR, allowing the RDMA NIC to saturate PCIe bandwidth without occupying compute units. The underlying storage is also optimized for random read/write of roughly 112KB blocks, with aggregate read peaks reaching 10TB per second. Of. course, there are always times when it's a miss, and this is where the changes in V 4.1 are most evident. In V 4.1, some layers use Sliding Window Attention (SWA), where each token only looks at the 128 tokens closest to it. The active block KV cache and state KV cache are stored in the inference card's VRAM. Blocks are paged every 128 tokens, with persistent parts written to the FS. The first 20 layers are maintained separately, each with a 128- token circular buffer, and an additional six reserved for speculative decoding. It is not synced, only kept in the memory of the machine that. generated it, and cleared after about three minutes. The hit rate is over 98% ; for cross-machine hits, it fetches data via a 400G network. So, what happens with the 2%that miss? V 4's approach is to recompute precisely, restoring the window state layer by layer. The number of tokens to recompute equals the number of layers multiplied by the window length. To reduce this, V4 also wrote this part of the cache to the disk, which ended up consuming nearly half of the disk cache capacity. The problem is that it is only useful for the few minutes of the conversation, so using a disk that can store data for several days is clearly not cost-effective. Therefore, V 4.1.

adopted a different approach called " SWAB," or "Sliding Window Approximation Boundary." It recomputes the last 128 tokens, and the attention during calculation is limited to these 128 tokens as well, allowing for an approximate window cache. This way, the recomputation cost becomes a constant, independent of the context length or the number of model layers. The same method is also applied to the 20 layers of the decoder. The window cache for these 20 layers had to be rebuilt every prefill; after the change, instead of processing the last 2560 tokens, it only needs to handle 128. The total prefill computation is reduced by nearly half. However, while the cache. solves the reading speed, the decoding speed also needs to be faster. Each computation step of the model was originally only able to generate one token. The idea behind speculative decoding is to have a lightweight draft model generate five consecutive tokens, then pass them to the large model for one-time verification. Correct guesses are accepted directly, and at the first incorrect position, the large model provides the correct answer. This way, one computation step can yield more than one token, but the verification process itself also consumes computational power. If all five drafts are verified, a lot of computation will be wasted on rejected guesses. DSI's self-developed system, DISBK, estimates the probability of each guess being accepted first, directing verification. budget toward more promising areas. Compared to verifying five tokens every step, dynamic verification reduces the number of checks per step by about 30%, while the average length of accepted tokens remains basically the same. In terms of throughput, actual online testing showed a 6%improvement. Another set of more detailed data shows that as the sequence count increases from 16 to 96, the gains rise from -1.5%to 11%, so this figure is conditional; not all workloads get faster. There is overhead hidden between the CPU and GPU; normally, the GPU must stop after finishing a step to wait for the CPU to update the state of the previous round. before scheduling the next, which causes recurring waits for requests generating thousands of tokens. DeepInfra’s approach is called zero-overhead batch scheduling; while the name implies no scheduling cost, it actually hides CPU work within the GPU’s computation time. When the GPU handles the forward pass and sampling for step N, the CPU is already preparing the prefill for step N + 1, while simultaneously processing earlier sampling results, allowing some tasks to be submitted to the GPU execution queue early, with dependencies managed by Streams and Events. This ahead-of-time scheduling brings new. issues: when the CPU schedules the next round, the previous results might be uncertain. Standard autoregressive decoding advances one token at a time, but with speculative decoding, a request might accept multiple candidates; if it already has 1,000 tokens cached and accepts three this round, the CPU won't know the final count, causing calculations—like query length, key length, and rotary positional encoding—to be skewed if using the old length. DeepInfra maintains a counter for tokens dispatched but not yet committed, reserving cache space in advance by accounting for in-flight calculations. Since request positions change between. consecutive rounds—with some ending, new ones joining, and others being preempted—it uses a mapping layer to align the current round's requests with the previous round's execution state, using device-side kernels to correct the lengths. Memory reclamation is also deferred. During synchronous execution, the CPU can release references once a request finishes, but that doesn't work in this pipeline. Even if a request has finished CPU post-processing, the GPU may still have operations using it, so DeepInfra queues the metadata, output objects, and cache blocks to be reclaimed, processing them at later.

synchronization points, with GPU-related resources verified using CUDA events. Synchronization issues also exist between multiple cards; the deployment scale for V 4.1 uses 2 to 8 for prefill, and 64 to 128 for decoding . With such wide expert parallelism, cards in the same communication domain must stay synchronized. Otherwise, if some are running prefill while others are still decoding, collective communication will fail. DPIN adds intra-group voting to the scheduler with two modes: one requires all cards to meet the conditions before switching , while the other allows partial card triggering to avoid small requests waiting too long. Afterward, there is a. second round of verification, because having requests in the queue doesn't guarantee they can be scheduled in this round; in practice, you may encounter situations where a card lacks cache capacity or sequence slots. After confirmation, if only some cards are assigned tasks, the others execute an empty prefill step; thus, expert load is another factor that drags down the computation of the entire round. V 4.1 is a typical MoE model with 384 routing experts in total; each token uses only six of them, plus one shared expert. When scaled to EP64, these experts are distributed across 64 cards, with six on each, plus a copy of a popular. expert; these seven do not include the shared expert. The fewer experts on each card, the fewer parameters need to be loaded from VRAM at each step, allowing the same number of cards to handle more requests. The copies of popular experts are not fixed either; load statistics are collected every 1,000 steps, and redistribution happens every 10,000 steps. Actual test results show the busiest card is only 9%higher than the average, so while residual imbalance remains, it has been kept quite low. Requests themselves must also be distributed evenly. For prefill , input lengths are divided into four tiers: under 16K, 16K to 64K, 64K to. 256K, and above 256K. The number of machines allocated to each tier is dynamically adjusted based on the previous round's demand. For decoding, it considers each card's request count and total cache length; short requests are assigned to cards with fewer requests and longer cache, while long requests go to cards with shorter cache . With this scheduling system, the performance reaches about 80%of the perfectly balanced state seen in offline testing. Load balancers are also categorized into four types, including one each for prefill, decoding, visual encoding, and expert parallelism; scaling is handled at the cluster level. Prefill monitors the number of cache-miss tokens, decoding looks at the number of requests. currently being processed, and scaling uses upper and lower bounds as well as count limits. In expert parallel deployment, the biggest fear is wasting long-tail requests. So, when a decoding instance receives a shutdown notice, it doesn't exit immediately; it allows a one-minute grace period. Anything unfinished is then passed on, along with the request and KV cache, to another instance to continue processing . Additionally, DeepSeek maintains a batch of pre-prepared but unallocated machines as a burst inventory pool. They trigger prohibitions when utilization rates exceed 0.8. Regarding fault tolerance, DeepSeek doesn't pursue extremely short restart times; they are actually in the minute range,. relying on capacity quotas and request re-routing to provide coverage. In an instance, all GPUs share the same communication domain. If one card fails , the entire instance stops working, so upon restart, they recount the healthy cards and re-determine the TP degree based on the actual available count. As for cross-datacenter operations, officials say it’s technically feasible. V 4.1 has significantly compressed the KV cache, requiring about 400Gbps of interconnect bandwidth per eight cards, but this sacrifices reliability, as fiber cables between datacenters can be cut. This is why DeepSeek places their own inference nodes in different but adjacent.

datacenters. With the technical side covered, it's time for us to crunch the numbers. DeepSeek has rarely disclosed their unit economics. They have a cluster performing 1.55 trillion tokens per day. Based on the stock price, each card earns an average of $ 38 per hour. Multiply that by 24 and then by 30, and each card makes about $ 27,000 per month—a figure rarely disclosed by peers. Liang Wenfeng once mentioned at a private investor meeting that their API pricing is based on a reasonable profit, aiming to recover the cost of a batch of equipment in about ten months. He stated that they only seek a reasonable profit, not profit. maximization. However, DeepSeek clearly intends to commercialize and must ultimately survive. At its core, it is still a company, just one that is considering which profits to pursue, when to make money, how to make it, and what trade-offs to make. If we look at these statements alongside the Coca-Cola story, many things seem to align. In 2011, when the Coca-Cola formula was leaked, almost nothing happened. The company claimed it was just an early draft and that the production version had been refined several times, so the stock price stayed flat while sales actually increased. Because Coca-Cola's moat was never the syrup formula, but its bottling and distribution network, brand perception, and cost discipline. DeepSeek's approach this time is a lot like Coca-Cola; they've made the recipe public, but the recipe isn't where the real money is made. So, what exactly are they after? The answer lies in the entry points and the formats. As the gap between flagship models narrows and it's hard to pull ahead based solely on parameters and leaderboards, the focus of competition is shifting from "whose model is stronger" to "who controls the entry points, data flows, and formats." Search and Feed are what they're fighting for: the entry points. Every time an agent searches for information, it has to call a tool; whoever is the default occupies that position, and any model can pass through that gateway. Every query, crawl, citation, and. selection can turn into training signals, creating a flywheel of entry points, data, models, and even stronger entry points. As for the recipe, it’s about grabbing the format; they turned their official processing logic into a public library, so third parties just follow it, and their behavior naturally aligns. This is certainly a good thing for developers, as agents tuned for official behavior won't easily run into issues when switching to other service providers. For DeepSeek, it’s even better; prompt formats, tool-calling formats, and streaming output rules will become the de facto industry standard as more third-party services adopt them. The reaction from the industry has been quite direct. The. official Llama account posted a message , thanking DeepSeek for contributing back to the community under the Apache 2.0 license, which was originally built on Llama. Researcher Chen Deli said on X that this is a duel between open source and closed source, and the other side can keep fighting as long as they want. DeepSeek-Harness lead Cui Tianyi put it more pragmatically: open sourcing is about hoping companies worldwide can deploy DeepSeek models and earn real revenue with them. Outside of this, others are calculating a different set of numbers. One blogger extrapolated from the extreme utilization of the GB200 NV72, suggesting one gigawatt of compute could generate $ 100 billion to $ 149. billion in annual revenue—nearly ten times higher than previous institutional forecasts. Others are calculating gross margins based on an hourly rental cost of $ 3 per GPU, assuming sufficiently high API usage. If calculated at a rental rate of $ 3 to $ 6, the rent only accounts for 6%to 12%of revenue. While these numbers sound impressive, they actually need to be taken with a grain of salt. The first two are built on optimistic assumptions, and the third only deducts GPU rent without accounting for storage , networking, inference, and R&D costs, and is also highly dependent on cache hit rates and traffic structure. Therefore, treating these as DeepSeek’s profit margins or payback.

periods just doesn't hold up. The 38 dollars refers to revenue, not profit, nor is it earnings generated solely by the DeepInf project. There is an even bigger limitation: what was open-sourced this time is the engine, not the chassis. The open-sourced DeepInf is clearly explained in the official README. Building a complete inference service still requires three things: an independent KV cache system, a vision encoder, facilities for pre-fill and decoding, and load balancing between data-parallel replicas. The documentation also admits that cache management and load balancing in a production environment are too deeply coupled with internal infrastructure and have not been fully. open-sourced for now. Therefore, while external teams can see how requests flow through the scheduler, cache communication, and sampling after getting the code, and can extract specific optimizations for their own use, replicating an online service that is both fast and efficient still requires them to tackle storage, networking, service management, and failover themselves. However, if you can get offline inference running, you are likely not far from a production system. Of course, hardware is another hurdle. The current support list only includes the NVIDIA SM100 and Huawei Ascend 910; the H100, H800, A100, and standard consumer-grade cards are not. included. The official recommendation is 64 cards for pre-fill and 64 for decoding. This is the starting scale for efficiency, not the baseline for just running it. For most teams, this suite is not yet a tool you can use immediately after downloading. Let's address the hardware part separately. At the bottom line, DeepSeek has released programming tools, compute libraries, and communication libraries for the Ascend platform, with the Huawei team providing R&D support. Regarding the scale, Bloomberg has reported that DeepSeek plans to deploy at least 160,000 Ascend 910 chips in its new Inner Mongolia data center. This is a planned figure and cannot be counted as the scale already in. operation. Additionally, performance tests in the README were conducted on NVIDIA SM100s. Having both chips on the support list does not mean they have achieved identical performance and costs. How, then, should we evaluate this? I think what is truly worth noting here is that DeepSeek has rarely assembled all these components together . Over the past few years, the outside world has only seen individual parts: FlashAttention for attention, GEMM for matrix operations, EP for expert communication, and EPLB for expert placement. Each component has its own papers and foundations, but how a request traverses them, and what the. intermediate data contracts look like, has always remained a black box. DPO puts these into the same public project ; although it doesn't grant full control, the overall assembly diagram is now visible. This also shows that model architecture is determining runtime structure. MLA, sliding windows , producer-consumer layer optimization, hyper-connected MoE, and multi-token prediction are not configurations that generic engines can auto-infer; they directly change cache layout, scheduler state machines, computation graph shapes, and retrieval logic. That is why DeepSeek had to write its own. engine rather than patching a generic framework. As for open source itself, I don't think it's as naive as idealism suggests, nor as dark as conspiracy theories claim. As the Wenzi says, "Do good with everyone, share skills so all may know," meaning good deeds should be done together, and capabilities should be accessible to all. Of course, there is a commercial calculation involved as well, but these two things are not in conflict. By going public, they gain access to entry points, standards, data flow, and scale—all of which are actually far more valuable than the recipe itself. The remaining question.

is, once inference engines and API formats become public goods, what will be left for model vendors to truly distinguish themselves? Is it data, use cases, or just like Coca-Cola, owning the refrigerator?

=============

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RNdnfCpQTZU

10月20日，DeepSeek 开源线上推理框架 DeepInfer 与协议编解码组件 deepseek-recipe，同时公开了单集群155万亿 Token、每卡每小时38美元这些线上数据。本期按一次请求的完整路径拆：预填充与解码分离、96%的缓存命中、3FS 上的KV缓存 分层、SWA 有界重放把预填充计算量砍掉近一半、DSpark 动态验证、零开销批调度、384个专家摊到64张卡；再往上看集群层，四类负载均衡器、扩缩容与1分钟下线宽限期、坏卡后重定 EP Size。也讲清开源边界：引擎给了，KV 存储、解耦设施和跨副本负载均衡没给，硬件只支持 SM100 和昇腾950。最后算一笔账，看它为什么像可口可乐。
item.description:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RNdnfCpQTZU

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入剖析 DeepSeek 開源的 DeepInf 推理架構，理解大模型從靜態權重轉化為高併發線上服務的工程內幕。
  • 掌握 PD 分離（Prefill 與 Decoding 分離）設計思維，了解如何依照算力與顯存頻寬需求，異質佈署高效能叢集。
  • 揭示巨幅降低推論成本的核心密碼：透過 KV Cache 前綴匹配與 3FS 分布式儲存，將吞吐效能提升 25 倍並兼顧系統容錯能力。

摘要

開源引擎的戰略轉變與三大組件佈局

作者大飛指出，DeepSeek 正式開源了支撐其線上服務的推論框架 DeepInf 與編碼組件 DeepSeek-Recipe。傳統觀點常認為模型開源僅是釋出權重檔案，但權重就像食譜，若沒有強大的後廚工程團隊（推論引擎）負責排隊與排程調度，便無法即時產出回答。過去 DeepSeek 曾因高度客製化與維護成本考量而不願開放內部引擎，如今不僅推翻前態全面開源，還聯同先前的 Search 與 Fetch 工具構建了完整閉環：由檢索工具抓取乾淨食材、DeepInf 統籌算力烹飪，並由 DeepSeek-Recipe 擔任翻譯多國語言訂單的菜單。

DeepSeek-Recipe 的協議轉換與防禦機制

為解決 OpenAI 與 Anthropic 等主流 API 格式互不相容的問題，以 Rust 打造的 DeepSeek-Recipe 提供了轉譯機制，將外部請求標準化為內部對話格式並編碼為 tokens。該組件內建跨資料區塊解析的狀態機，解決 UTF-8 中文字與工具參數在資料流中被切碎的問題。此外，Recipe 僅在建構 Prompt 時將結構標籤映射為特殊標籤，若使用者手動輸入相同字元則視為普通文字，巧妙修補了假冒系統指令的注入漏洞，同時支援開啟思考模式下最高 131,072 tokens 的深度推理輸出。

PD 分離架構與硬體極致調度

在推論生命週期中，運算被嚴格拆分為 Prefill（預填） 與 Decoding（解碼） 兩大階段。Prefill 需要一次性吸收大量歷史紀錄與系統提示，極度消耗純算力；Decoding 則是逐字生成，效能瓶頸在於自顯存讀取參數與快取的頻寬。DeepSeek 藉此落實了徹底的 PD 分離：Prefill 採用 8 卡伺服器集中攻堅，Decoding 分配給 64 至 128 卡的運算叢集，而視覺編碼器則獨立交由廉價單卡處理。透過針對不同特性的階段配置相應硬體，實現了首字延遲與接續輸出速率的最佳化。

KV Cache 前綴快取與 3FS 分布式儲存架構

在多輪對話與 Agent 工具調用中，重複傳輸的歷史脈絡耗費巨大，DeepSeek 透過 KV Cache 前綴匹配 實現極致省流。命中快取後，單卡 Prefill 吞吐量能從每秒 6 萬 tokens 激增至 150 萬 tokens，成本僅需未命中的五十分之一。這些快取被統一存放在容量達 100PB 的 3FS 分布式儲存系統 中，針對對話流量保留長達七天以捕捉長尾命中率。計算與儲存分離的架構不僅消除了單機故障遺失快取的風險，更結合 GDR 與 RDMA 技術，在運算進行時無縫搬移資料，將推論成本與延遲壓榨至極限。

================================================

Hello everyone, welcome to Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. On October 20th , DeepSeek open-sourced its inference framework, DeepInf, which powers its online services, along with its companion encoding component, DeepSeek-Recipe. This time, DeepSeek didn’t release a new model or climb the leaderboards; instead, they handed over the blueprints for the engine behind the model. Today, let’s talk about this framework. To understand it, we first need to clarify what an inference framework actually is. Many think open-sourcing a model just means downloading the weights, and that's it. But weights are just a pile of numbers; they can't talk or answer questions. In. between lies an entire engineering stack responsible for queuing requests, feeding them into the chips, and retrieving the results. Tech blogger Baoyu once used the analogy of a cookbook and a kitchen staff. If the model file is the recipe, the inference framework is the kitchen staff. Give the same recipe to different kitchen crews, and the number of orders they can handle per hour—and how long customers wait—can vary significantly . That’s why open-sourcing an engine is much rarer than open-sourcing weights. Open weights are now routine, but open-sourcing an engine means showing everyone how you staff your kitchen and how you scale operations. In April 2025, DeepSeek explained why they wouldn’t open their internal engine, essentially saying it was heavily customized for their environment and hard to migrate, and that the team didn't have the resources to maintain a large public project. However, by this October, they overturned that stance. They released more than one repository; besides DeepInf, there’s also DeepSeek-Recipe . Just a few days before that, DeepSeek launched Search and Fetch tools specifically for models. While these three things seem scattered, they are actually connected. Search and Fetch go out to source ingredients, DeepInf is the kitchen crew, and Recipe serves as. a multi-lingual menu, allowing orders in various formats to be translated into a language the kitchen understands . Let’s briefly touch on Search and Fetch, which are backed by a layer people rarely consider. We all know search engines are designed for humans, filled with ads, recommendations, and pop-ups that we can easily ignore. But models can’t; every extra word consumes context, uses tokens, and costs money. These two APIs return raw JSON data. Beyond providing titles, URLs, summaries, full text, and timestamps, they also include relevance. and authority scores. It’s quite simple: you provide a URL, and it returns cleaned-up Markdown data. The two APIs are priced at 5 yuan per 1,000 successful requests, and users can call them using server-side tools in depsharnessCodecodex. There is no charge before November 1, 2026, at 0:00 Beijing Time. It also doesn't require binding a specific model; you only need a Depsik API to call models from other providers. Of course, the real star is deepINF, which adopts the Apache 2.0 license. It supports NVIDIA's SM100 and Huawei's Ascend 950, requiring a Linux. environment with Python 3.12 and GCC 13 or higher. On the NVIDIA side, it requires CUDA 13, and for Ascend, it needs CANN 9.2. Currently, it only supports one model: depsicv 4.1 flash, with the weight code for pulling being depsicv 4.1 flash 1017. We will go into the specific logging details later. Next is deepsicrecipe, which solves format issues. Currently, there are three mainstream APIs: OpenAI chat completions and responses, as well as Anthropic messages. Ultimately, they all ask the model for answers, but the formats differ, so you cannot directly.

port the same conversation. If you want to run deepsake on your own server but write the client based on OpenAI standards, the model won't understand. Therefore, a translator is needed in between. RP handles this translation; its core is written in Rust, with a Python interface provided. It unifies all three types of requests into an internal conversation format, constructs prompts according to the model version, and encodes them into tokens using its built-in tokenizer. After the model outputs, it restores the tokens back into a response following the corresponding protocol and streams it back to the user. It also maintains a cross-data-block parsing state machine. Since a Chinese. character takes three bytes in UTF-8, it could be split across two adjacent blocks, as could tool parameters. Thus, it waits for data before parsing, ensuring the user never sees half a character. It also happens to patch a security vulnerability. Deps models rely on a set of special tokens to mark conversation structures, such as where a user's statement begins or when a tool is called. If someone manually types the exact same user or image tags in their input, they could impersonate the system and issue commands. Recipe's approach is to only map tags explicitly inserted during prompt construction. into special tokens; the same strings typed by a user are treated as ordinary text. Additionally, when thinking mode is disabled, the output limit defaults to 8,192 tokens. With thinking mode enabled, it is 65,536, and if the reasoning intensity is set to maximum, it can reach 131,072. Now, let’s look at an example to see how a request goes through the entire process. First, a request must pass through the tokenizer to become tokens, then it splits into two stages. The first stage is called prefill, where the model reads system prompts, chat history, and document. questions all at once; each token generates a set of intermediate results at every layer, known as the KV cache. The second stage is decoding, where it generates one token at a time; each new token produced requires using all the previous KV caches. These two stages consume completely different resources: prefill processes tens of thousands of tokens at once, demanding pure compute power, while decoding generates one token at a time, spending most of its time reading parameters and cache from VRAM. Therefore, DeepSeek splits them onto different machines, which is the commonly known PD separation. When this system was designed, three goals were set: compatibility with different. vendors 'chips, enabling commodity hardware for prefill and decoding, and keeping the KV cache for at least an hour. In deployment, prefill uses 8-GPU servers, decoding uses 64 to 128-GPU clusters, and the vision encoder is pulled out separately; each of the three stages gets its own resources, optimizing first-token and inter-token latency separately. The official documentation has an interesting note: the vision encoder usually only needs a single card, and they suggest using the cheapest available card. In actual deployment, the ratio of cards for the two stages is close to 1: 1; while a. minimum setup of one prefill unit and one decoding unit can run, efficient performance requires following the official starting scale. Next is the most cost-saving part of the entire system. In agent scenarios, every time a tool is called, the client must resend the complete history—system prompts, tool definitions, and every previous response and tool result—not a single bit can be missed. Yet, the vast majority of these have actually been calculated in the previous turn. DeepSeek’s approach is to cache the computed KV values, so in the next turn , it only calculates the newly added tokens. The requirement is that the prefix must match exactly to hit the.

cache, so it must align from the first token; repeated content starting in the middle cannot be used. How dramatic is the effect of this caching? On the same card, without cache hits, prefill can process 60,000 tokens per second; with cache hits, it’s 1.5 million—a 25- fold difference. The average input per request for Deps online is 77K, with an average time-to-first-token latency of 400ms, and a P99 of 1000ms. The cost of input with a cache hit is only 1/50th of a miss; for every point the hit rate increases, the bill gets thinner. These caches aren't stored in the compute machine's own memory, but in an independent storage cluster using. DeepSeg's previously open-sourced distributed file system, 3FS, with a capacity of about 100PB on SSDs, writing KV caches in blocks of 128 tokens. Cache for ENT traffic is kept for three days, while chat traffic is kept for seven days. Chat traffic is kept longer due to its long-tail hit characteristics, where a small amount of cache is read repeatedly, so losing it has a bigger impact on the overall hit rate. Based on Deck's estimates, if they only kept it for three days, the chat traffic hit rate would drop by 0.5 %to 1%. Looking at the industry, OpenAI and Google only keep caches for about 5 minutes to 24 hours, so three to seven. days is considered quite long. Storing them in an independent cluster has two benefits: any compute machine can read any piece of cache, so users are no longer locked to the previous machine. The failure rate of compute machines is also several orders of magnitude higher than storage, so even if a machine crashes, the cache remains. However, reading the cache shouldn't drag down the time-to-first-token latency, so DPS divides hits into three stages: the first stage, at the ingress service, uses a hash chain to perform prefix matching on the local KV store to get metadata. To hit the length, the second stage must fetch the data before. routing, using an independent process to move the cache from 3FS into host shared memory, while the third stage, the engine layer, moves it from shared memory to VRAM, overlapping layer-by-layer transfer with forward computation. They could have used a large copy engine, but the copy performance for fine-grained blocks wasn't ideal, so DPS switched to GDR, allowing the RDMA NIC to saturate PCIe bandwidth without occupying compute units. The underlying storage is also optimized for random read/write of roughly 112KB blocks, with aggregate read peaks reaching 10TB per second. Of. course, there are always times when it's a miss, and this is where the changes in V 4.1 are most evident. In V 4.1, some layers use Sliding Window Attention (SWA), where each token only looks at the 128 tokens closest to it. The active block KV cache and state KV cache are stored in the inference card's VRAM. Blocks are paged every 128 tokens, with persistent parts written to the FS. The first 20 layers are maintained separately, each with a 128- token circular buffer, and an additional six reserved for speculative decoding. It is not synced, only kept in the memory of the machine that. generated it, and cleared after about three minutes. The hit rate is over 98% ; for cross-machine hits, it fetches data via a 400G network. So, what happens with the 2%that miss? V 4's approach is to recompute precisely, restoring the window state layer by layer. The number of tokens to recompute equals the number of layers multiplied by the window length. To reduce this, V4 also wrote this part of the cache to the disk, which ended up consuming nearly half of the disk cache capacity. The problem is that it is only useful for the few minutes of the conversation, so using a disk that can store data for several days is clearly not cost-effective. Therefore, V 4.1.

adopted a different approach called " SWAB," or "Sliding Window Approximation Boundary." It recomputes the last 128 tokens, and the attention during calculation is limited to these 128 tokens as well, allowing for an approximate window cache. This way, the recomputation cost becomes a constant, independent of the context length or the number of model layers. The same method is also applied to the 20 layers of the decoder. The window cache for these 20 layers had to be rebuilt every prefill; after the change, instead of processing the last 2560 tokens, it only needs to handle 128. The total prefill computation is reduced by nearly half. However, while the cache. solves the reading speed, the decoding speed also needs to be faster. Each computation step of the model was originally only able to generate one token. The idea behind speculative decoding is to have a lightweight draft model generate five consecutive tokens, then pass them to the large model for one-time verification. Correct guesses are accepted directly, and at the first incorrect position, the large model provides the correct answer. This way, one computation step can yield more than one token, but the verification process itself also consumes computational power. If all five drafts are verified, a lot of computation will be wasted on rejected guesses. DSI's self-developed system, DISBK, estimates the probability of each guess being accepted first, directing verification. budget toward more promising areas. Compared to verifying five tokens every step, dynamic verification reduces the number of checks per step by about 30%, while the average length of accepted tokens remains basically the same. In terms of throughput, actual online testing showed a 6%improvement. Another set of more detailed data shows that as the sequence count increases from 16 to 96, the gains rise from -1.5%to 11%, so this figure is conditional; not all workloads get faster. There is overhead hidden between the CPU and GPU; normally, the GPU must stop after finishing a step to wait for the CPU to update the state of the previous round. before scheduling the next, which causes recurring waits for requests generating thousands of tokens. DeepInfra’s approach is called zero-overhead batch scheduling; while the name implies no scheduling cost, it actually hides CPU work within the GPU’s computation time. When the GPU handles the forward pass and sampling for step N, the CPU is already preparing the prefill for step N + 1, while simultaneously processing earlier sampling results, allowing some tasks to be submitted to the GPU execution queue early, with dependencies managed by Streams and Events. This ahead-of-time scheduling brings new. issues: when the CPU schedules the next round, the previous results might be uncertain. Standard autoregressive decoding advances one token at a time, but with speculative decoding, a request might accept multiple candidates; if it already has 1,000 tokens cached and accepts three this round, the CPU won't know the final count, causing calculations—like query length, key length, and rotary positional encoding—to be skewed if using the old length. DeepInfra maintains a counter for tokens dispatched but not yet committed, reserving cache space in advance by accounting for in-flight calculations. Since request positions change between. consecutive rounds—with some ending, new ones joining, and others being preempted—it uses a mapping layer to align the current round's requests with the previous round's execution state, using device-side kernels to correct the lengths. Memory reclamation is also deferred. During synchronous execution, the CPU can release references once a request finishes, but that doesn't work in this pipeline. Even if a request has finished CPU post-processing, the GPU may still have operations using it, so DeepInfra queues the metadata, output objects, and cache blocks to be reclaimed, processing them at later.

synchronization points, with GPU-related resources verified using CUDA events. Synchronization issues also exist between multiple cards; the deployment scale for V 4.1 uses 2 to 8 for prefill, and 64 to 128 for decoding . With such wide expert parallelism, cards in the same communication domain must stay synchronized. Otherwise, if some are running prefill while others are still decoding, collective communication will fail. DPIN adds intra-group voting to the scheduler with two modes: one requires all cards to meet the conditions before switching , while the other allows partial card triggering to avoid small requests waiting too long. Afterward, there is a. second round of verification, because having requests in the queue doesn't guarantee they can be scheduled in this round; in practice, you may encounter situations where a card lacks cache capacity or sequence slots. After confirmation, if only some cards are assigned tasks, the others execute an empty prefill step; thus, expert load is another factor that drags down the computation of the entire round. V 4.1 is a typical MoE model with 384 routing experts in total; each token uses only six of them, plus one shared expert. When scaled to EP64, these experts are distributed across 64 cards, with six on each, plus a copy of a popular. expert; these seven do not include the shared expert. The fewer experts on each card, the fewer parameters need to be loaded from VRAM at each step, allowing the same number of cards to handle more requests. The copies of popular experts are not fixed either; load statistics are collected every 1,000 steps, and redistribution happens every 10,000 steps. Actual test results show the busiest card is only 9%higher than the average, so while residual imbalance remains, it has been kept quite low. Requests themselves must also be distributed evenly. For prefill , input lengths are divided into four tiers: under 16K, 16K to 64K, 64K to. 256K, and above 256K. The number of machines allocated to each tier is dynamically adjusted based on the previous round's demand. For decoding, it considers each card's request count and total cache length; short requests are assigned to cards with fewer requests and longer cache, while long requests go to cards with shorter cache . With this scheduling system, the performance reaches about 80%of the perfectly balanced state seen in offline testing. Load balancers are also categorized into four types, including one each for prefill, decoding, visual encoding, and expert parallelism; scaling is handled at the cluster level. Prefill monitors the number of cache-miss tokens, decoding looks at the number of requests. currently being processed, and scaling uses upper and lower bounds as well as count limits. In expert parallel deployment, the biggest fear is wasting long-tail requests. So, when a decoding instance receives a shutdown notice, it doesn't exit immediately; it allows a one-minute grace period. Anything unfinished is then passed on, along with the request and KV cache, to another instance to continue processing . Additionally, DeepSeek maintains a batch of pre-prepared but unallocated machines as a burst inventory pool. They trigger prohibitions when utilization rates exceed 0.8. Regarding fault tolerance, DeepSeek doesn't pursue extremely short restart times; they are actually in the minute range,. relying on capacity quotas and request re-routing to provide coverage. In an instance, all GPUs share the same communication domain. If one card fails , the entire instance stops working, so upon restart, they recount the healthy cards and re-determine the TP degree based on the actual available count. As for cross-datacenter operations, officials say it’s technically feasible. V 4.1 has significantly compressed the KV cache, requiring about 400Gbps of interconnect bandwidth per eight cards, but this sacrifices reliability, as fiber cables between datacenters can be cut. This is why DeepSeek places their own inference nodes in different but adjacent.

datacenters. With the technical side covered, it's time for us to crunch the numbers. DeepSeek has rarely disclosed their unit economics. They have a cluster performing 1.55 trillion tokens per day. Based on the stock price, each card earns an average of $ 38 per hour. Multiply that by 24 and then by 30, and each card makes about $ 27,000 per month—a figure rarely disclosed by peers. Liang Wenfeng once mentioned at a private investor meeting that their API pricing is based on a reasonable profit, aiming to recover the cost of a batch of equipment in about ten months. He stated that they only seek a reasonable profit, not profit. maximization. However, DeepSeek clearly intends to commercialize and must ultimately survive. At its core, it is still a company, just one that is considering which profits to pursue, when to make money, how to make it, and what trade-offs to make. If we look at these statements alongside the Coca-Cola story, many things seem to align. In 2011, when the Coca-Cola formula was leaked, almost nothing happened. The company claimed it was just an early draft and that the production version had been refined several times, so the stock price stayed flat while sales actually increased. Because Coca-Cola's moat was never the syrup formula, but its bottling and distribution network, brand perception, and cost discipline. DeepSeek's approach this time is a lot like Coca-Cola; they've made the recipe public, but the recipe isn't where the real money is made. So, what exactly are they after? The answer lies in the entry points and the formats. As the gap between flagship models narrows and it's hard to pull ahead based solely on parameters and leaderboards, the focus of competition is shifting from "whose model is stronger" to "who controls the entry points, data flows, and formats." Search and Feed are what they're fighting for: the entry points. Every time an agent searches for information, it has to call a tool; whoever is the default occupies that position, and any model can pass through that gateway. Every query, crawl, citation, and. selection can turn into training signals, creating a flywheel of entry points, data, models, and even stronger entry points. As for the recipe, it’s about grabbing the format; they turned their official processing logic into a public library, so third parties just follow it, and their behavior naturally aligns. This is certainly a good thing for developers, as agents tuned for official behavior won't easily run into issues when switching to other service providers. For DeepSeek, it’s even better; prompt formats, tool-calling formats, and streaming output rules will become the de facto industry standard as more third-party services adopt them. The reaction from the industry has been quite direct. The. official Llama account posted a message , thanking DeepSeek for contributing back to the community under the Apache 2.0 license, which was originally built on Llama. Researcher Chen Deli said on X that this is a duel between open source and closed source, and the other side can keep fighting as long as they want. DeepSeek-Harness lead Cui Tianyi put it more pragmatically: open sourcing is about hoping companies worldwide can deploy DeepSeek models and earn real revenue with them. Outside of this, others are calculating a different set of numbers. One blogger extrapolated from the extreme utilization of the GB200 NV72, suggesting one gigawatt of compute could generate $ 100 billion to $ 149. billion in annual revenue—nearly ten times higher than previous institutional forecasts. Others are calculating gross margins based on an hourly rental cost of $ 3 per GPU, assuming sufficiently high API usage. If calculated at a rental rate of $ 3 to $ 6, the rent only accounts for 6%to 12%of revenue. While these numbers sound impressive, they actually need to be taken with a grain of salt. The first two are built on optimistic assumptions, and the third only deducts GPU rent without accounting for storage , networking, inference, and R&D costs, and is also highly dependent on cache hit rates and traffic structure. Therefore, treating these as DeepSeek’s profit margins or payback.

periods just doesn't hold up. The 38 dollars refers to revenue, not profit, nor is it earnings generated solely by the DeepInf project. There is an even bigger limitation: what was open-sourced this time is the engine, not the chassis. The open-sourced DeepInf is clearly explained in the official README. Building a complete inference service still requires three things: an independent KV cache system, a vision encoder, facilities for pre-fill and decoding, and load balancing between data-parallel replicas. The documentation also admits that cache management and load balancing in a production environment are too deeply coupled with internal infrastructure and have not been fully. open-sourced for now. Therefore, while external teams can see how requests flow through the scheduler, cache communication, and sampling after getting the code, and can extract specific optimizations for their own use, replicating an online service that is both fast and efficient still requires them to tackle storage, networking, service management, and failover themselves. However, if you can get offline inference running, you are likely not far from a production system. Of course, hardware is another hurdle. The current support list only includes the NVIDIA SM100 and Huawei Ascend 910; the H100, H800, A100, and standard consumer-grade cards are not. included. The official recommendation is 64 cards for pre-fill and 64 for decoding. This is the starting scale for efficiency, not the baseline for just running it. For most teams, this suite is not yet a tool you can use immediately after downloading. Let's address the hardware part separately. At the bottom line, DeepSeek has released programming tools, compute libraries, and communication libraries for the Ascend platform, with the Huawei team providing R&D support. Regarding the scale, Bloomberg has reported that DeepSeek plans to deploy at least 160,000 Ascend 910 chips in its new Inner Mongolia data center. This is a planned figure and cannot be counted as the scale already in. operation. Additionally, performance tests in the README were conducted on NVIDIA SM100s. Having both chips on the support list does not mean they have achieved identical performance and costs. How, then, should we evaluate this? I think what is truly worth noting here is that DeepSeek has rarely assembled all these components together . Over the past few years, the outside world has only seen individual parts: FlashAttention for attention, GEMM for matrix operations, EP for expert communication, and EPLB for expert placement. Each component has its own papers and foundations, but how a request traverses them, and what the. intermediate data contracts look like, has always remained a black box. DPO puts these into the same public project ; although it doesn't grant full control, the overall assembly diagram is now visible. This also shows that model architecture is determining runtime structure. MLA, sliding windows , producer-consumer layer optimization, hyper-connected MoE, and multi-token prediction are not configurations that generic engines can auto-infer; they directly change cache layout, scheduler state machines, computation graph shapes, and retrieval logic. That is why DeepSeek had to write its own. engine rather than patching a generic framework. As for open source itself, I don't think it's as naive as idealism suggests, nor as dark as conspiracy theories claim. As the Wenzi says, "Do good with everyone, share skills so all may know," meaning good deeds should be done together, and capabilities should be accessible to all. Of course, there is a commercial calculation involved as well, but these two things are not in conflict. By going public, they gain access to entry points, standards, data flow, and scale—all of which are actually far more valuable than the recipe itself. The remaining question.

is, once inference engines and API formats become public goods, what will be left for model vendors to truly distinguish themselves? Is it data, use cases, or just like Coca-Cola, owning the refrigerator?

=============

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RNdnfCpQTZU

10月20日，DeepSeek 开源线上推理框架 DeepInfer 与协议编解码组件 deepseek-recipe，同时公开了单集群155万亿 Token、每卡每小时38美元这些线上数据。本期按一次请求的完整路径拆：预填充与解码分离、96%的缓存命中、3FS 上的KV缓存 分层、SWA 有界重放把预填充计算量砍掉近一半、DSpark 动态验证、零开销批调度、384个专家摊到64张卡；再往上看集群层，四类负载均衡器、扩缩容与1分钟下线宽限期、坏卡后重定 EP Size。也讲清开源边界：引擎给了，KV 存储、解耦设施和跨副本负载均衡没给，硬件只支持 SM100 和昇腾950。最后算一笔账，看它为什么像可口可乐。
item.content:encoded:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RNdnfCpQTZU

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入剖析 DeepSeek 開源的 DeepInf 推理架構，理解大模型從靜態權重轉化為高併發線上服務的工程內幕。
  • 掌握 PD 分離（Prefill 與 Decoding 分離）設計思維，了解如何依照算力與顯存頻寬需求，異質佈署高效能叢集。
  • 揭示巨幅降低推論成本的核心密碼：透過 KV Cache 前綴匹配與 3FS 分布式儲存，將吞吐效能提升 25 倍並兼顧系統容錯能力。

摘要

開源引擎的戰略轉變與三大組件佈局

作者大飛指出，DeepSeek 正式開源了支撐其線上服務的推論框架 DeepInf 與編碼組件 DeepSeek-Recipe。傳統觀點常認為模型開源僅是釋出權重檔案，但權重就像食譜，若沒有強大的後廚工程團隊（推論引擎）負責排隊與排程調度，便無法即時產出回答。過去 DeepSeek 曾因高度客製化與維護成本考量而不願開放內部引擎，如今不僅推翻前態全面開源，還聯同先前的 Search 與 Fetch 工具構建了完整閉環：由檢索工具抓取乾淨食材、DeepInf 統籌算力烹飪，並由 DeepSeek-Recipe 擔任翻譯多國語言訂單的菜單。

DeepSeek-Recipe 的協議轉換與防禦機制

為解決 OpenAI 與 Anthropic 等主流 API 格式互不相容的問題，以 Rust 打造的 DeepSeek-Recipe 提供了轉譯機制，將外部請求標準化為內部對話格式並編碼為 tokens。該組件內建跨資料區塊解析的狀態機，解決 UTF-8 中文字與工具參數在資料流中被切碎的問題。此外，Recipe 僅在建構 Prompt 時將結構標籤映射為特殊標籤，若使用者手動輸入相同字元則視為普通文字，巧妙修補了假冒系統指令的注入漏洞，同時支援開啟思考模式下最高 131,072 tokens 的深度推理輸出。

PD 分離架構與硬體極致調度

在推論生命週期中，運算被嚴格拆分為 Prefill（預填） 與 Decoding（解碼） 兩大階段。Prefill 需要一次性吸收大量歷史紀錄與系統提示，極度消耗純算力；Decoding 則是逐字生成，效能瓶頸在於自顯存讀取參數與快取的頻寬。DeepSeek 藉此落實了徹底的 PD 分離：Prefill 採用 8 卡伺服器集中攻堅，Decoding 分配給 64 至 128 卡的運算叢集，而視覺編碼器則獨立交由廉價單卡處理。透過針對不同特性的階段配置相應硬體，實現了首字延遲與接續輸出速率的最佳化。

KV Cache 前綴快取與 3FS 分布式儲存架構

在多輪對話與 Agent 工具調用中，重複傳輸的歷史脈絡耗費巨大，DeepSeek 透過 KV Cache 前綴匹配 實現極致省流。命中快取後，單卡 Prefill 吞吐量能從每秒 6 萬 tokens 激增至 150 萬 tokens，成本僅需未命中的五十分之一。這些快取被統一存放在容量達 100PB 的 3FS 分布式儲存系統 中，針對對話流量保留長達七天以捕捉長尾命中率。計算與儲存分離的架構不僅消除了單機故障遺失快取的風險，更結合 GDR 與 RDMA 技術，在運算進行時無縫搬移資料，將推論成本與延遲壓榨至極限。

================================================

Hello everyone, welcome to Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. On October 20th , DeepSeek open-sourced its inference framework, DeepInf, which powers its online services, along with its companion encoding component, DeepSeek-Recipe. This time, DeepSeek didn’t release a new model or climb the leaderboards; instead, they handed over the blueprints for the engine behind the model. Today, let’s talk about this framework. To understand it, we first need to clarify what an inference framework actually is. Many think open-sourcing a model just means downloading the weights, and that's it. But weights are just a pile of numbers; they can't talk or answer questions. In. between lies an entire engineering stack responsible for queuing requests, feeding them into the chips, and retrieving the results. Tech blogger Baoyu once used the analogy of a cookbook and a kitchen staff. If the model file is the recipe, the inference framework is the kitchen staff. Give the same recipe to different kitchen crews, and the number of orders they can handle per hour—and how long customers wait—can vary significantly . That’s why open-sourcing an engine is much rarer than open-sourcing weights. Open weights are now routine, but open-sourcing an engine means showing everyone how you staff your kitchen and how you scale operations. In April 2025, DeepSeek explained why they wouldn’t open their internal engine, essentially saying it was heavily customized for their environment and hard to migrate, and that the team didn't have the resources to maintain a large public project. However, by this October, they overturned that stance. They released more than one repository; besides DeepInf, there’s also DeepSeek-Recipe . Just a few days before that, DeepSeek launched Search and Fetch tools specifically for models. While these three things seem scattered, they are actually connected. Search and Fetch go out to source ingredients, DeepInf is the kitchen crew, and Recipe serves as. a multi-lingual menu, allowing orders in various formats to be translated into a language the kitchen understands . Let’s briefly touch on Search and Fetch, which are backed by a layer people rarely consider. We all know search engines are designed for humans, filled with ads, recommendations, and pop-ups that we can easily ignore. But models can’t; every extra word consumes context, uses tokens, and costs money. These two APIs return raw JSON data. Beyond providing titles, URLs, summaries, full text, and timestamps, they also include relevance. and authority scores. It’s quite simple: you provide a URL, and it returns cleaned-up Markdown data. The two APIs are priced at 5 yuan per 1,000 successful requests, and users can call them using server-side tools in depsharnessCodecodex. There is no charge before November 1, 2026, at 0:00 Beijing Time. It also doesn't require binding a specific model; you only need a Depsik API to call models from other providers. Of course, the real star is deepINF, which adopts the Apache 2.0 license. It supports NVIDIA's SM100 and Huawei's Ascend 950, requiring a Linux. environment with Python 3.12 and GCC 13 or higher. On the NVIDIA side, it requires CUDA 13, and for Ascend, it needs CANN 9.2. Currently, it only supports one model: depsicv 4.1 flash, with the weight code for pulling being depsicv 4.1 flash 1017. We will go into the specific logging details later. Next is deepsicrecipe, which solves format issues. Currently, there are three mainstream APIs: OpenAI chat completions and responses, as well as Anthropic messages. Ultimately, they all ask the model for answers, but the formats differ, so you cannot directly.

port the same conversation. If you want to run deepsake on your own server but write the client based on OpenAI standards, the model won't understand. Therefore, a translator is needed in between. RP handles this translation; its core is written in Rust, with a Python interface provided. It unifies all three types of requests into an internal conversation format, constructs prompts according to the model version, and encodes them into tokens using its built-in tokenizer. After the model outputs, it restores the tokens back into a response following the corresponding protocol and streams it back to the user. It also maintains a cross-data-block parsing state machine. Since a Chinese. character takes three bytes in UTF-8, it could be split across two adjacent blocks, as could tool parameters. Thus, it waits for data before parsing, ensuring the user never sees half a character. It also happens to patch a security vulnerability. Deps models rely on a set of special tokens to mark conversation structures, such as where a user's statement begins or when a tool is called. If someone manually types the exact same user or image tags in their input, they could impersonate the system and issue commands. Recipe's approach is to only map tags explicitly inserted during prompt construction. into special tokens; the same strings typed by a user are treated as ordinary text. Additionally, when thinking mode is disabled, the output limit defaults to 8,192 tokens. With thinking mode enabled, it is 65,536, and if the reasoning intensity is set to maximum, it can reach 131,072. Now, let’s look at an example to see how a request goes through the entire process. First, a request must pass through the tokenizer to become tokens, then it splits into two stages. The first stage is called prefill, where the model reads system prompts, chat history, and document. questions all at once; each token generates a set of intermediate results at every layer, known as the KV cache. The second stage is decoding, where it generates one token at a time; each new token produced requires using all the previous KV caches. These two stages consume completely different resources: prefill processes tens of thousands of tokens at once, demanding pure compute power, while decoding generates one token at a time, spending most of its time reading parameters and cache from VRAM.
